They distort the Scripture, taking rulings out of context, then say, “If this is the ruling you get ˹from Muḥammad˺, accept it. If not, beware!” Whoever Allah allows to be deluded, you can never be of any help to them against Allah. It is not Allah’s Will to purify their hearts. For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter

**Do Not Grieve for Those Who Race to Disbelief**

Yā ayyuhā al-rasūl lā yaḥzunka alladhīna yusāri'ūna fī al-kufr consoles Messenger. Lā yaḥzunka, do not grieve you, yaḥzun from ḥ-z-n, to grieve, and yusāri'ūna fī al-kufr, race to disbelief, from s-r-', to be quick, race, indicates they hasten to disbelief, competing in it. The phrase appears also in *“Do not grieve for those who race to disbelief”* (5:41) itself and in *“Those who race to disbelief will not harm Allah”* (3:176). The racing shows eagerness, not reluctance. Two groups are described: those who say we believe with tongues but hearts disbelieve, munāfiqūn, hypocrites, and Jews who listen to lies. The first group says āmannā bi-afwāhihim wa lam tu'min qulūbuhum — we believe with mouths but hearts did not believe — showing contradiction between tongue and heart. The second, samā'ūna li-l-kadhib, eager listeners to lies, from s-m-', to listen, and kadhib, lie, indicates they listen to falsehood and accept it. The verse tells Prophet ﷺ not to grieve because their racing does not harm Allah or Messenger, only themselves.

**Distorting Scripture Taking Rulings Out of Context**

Yuḥarrifūna al-kalim min ba'di mawāḍi'ihi — they distort words after they have been placed — similar to verse 13 but with min ba'di, after places, indicating distortion after proper placement. They take rulings out of context, then say in ūtītum hādhā fa-khudhūhu wa in lam tu'tawhu fa-iḥdharū — if you are given this, take it, if not, beware — showing they pick and choose rulings based on desire, not truth. This is precisely taking ruling out of context and following desire, as verse 48 will warn *“Do not follow their desires”* (5:48).

**Hearts Not Purified, Disgrace and Tremendous Punishment**

Ulā'ika alladhīna lam yuridi Allāhu a yuṭahhira qulūbahum — they are those whose hearts Allah did not will to purify — indicates that purification of heart requires divine will plus human effort; when humans persistently choose lies and distortion, Allah does not will to purify. Qulūb, hearts, purification is needed because heart is source of belief, as *“In hearts is disease”* (2:10) for hypocrites. Lahum fī al-dunyā khizyun wa lahum fī al-ākhirati 'adhābun 'aẓīm — for them disgrace in world and tremendous punishment in Hereafter — shows two-level consequence: khizy, disgrace, in world, through exposure of lies and failure, and 'adhāb 'aẓīm, tremendous punishment, in Hereafter. The same closing appears in verse 33 for ḥirābah and here for distortion, showing that distorting scripture and racing to disbelief is also grave. The verse therefore consoles Messenger that their disgrace is already beginning, and tremendous punishment awaits, so grief is unnecessary.

The stoning incident is verified as occasion of revelation: Jewish couple committed adultery, Jewish leaders brought them to Prophet ﷺ hoping for lighter penalty, Prophet asked about Torah ruling, they hid stoning verse, 'Abdullāh ibn Salām exposed it, Prophet ordered stoning, as recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (3635) and Muslim (1699). The verse's description yuḥarrifūna al-kalim min ba'di mawāḍi'ihi matches that hiding. The phrase samā'ūna li-l-kadhib, listeners to lies, is interpreted as listening to false rabbis who permit lies. The verse's consolation lā yaḥzunka is also in *“Do not grieve for those who race to disbelief”* (3:176) for similar context, showing consistent prophetic consolation. The next verse will discuss listening to falsehood and consuming forbidden gain, continuing description of same group.
verses.42:
> They eagerly listen to falsehood and consume forbidden gain. So if they come to you ˹O Prophet˺, either judge between them or turn away from them. If you turn away from them, they cannot harm you whatsoever. But if you judge between them, then do so with justice. Surely Allah loves those who are just

**If You Turn Away They Cannot Harm You**

Wa in tu'riḍ 'anhum fa-lan yaḍurrūka shay'an — if you turn away from them, they cannot harm you at all — reassures. Tu'riḍ, turn away, yaḍurrūka, harm you, from ḍ-r-r, to harm, shay'an, anything, indicates that their plots cannot harm Prophet if he turns away, because Allah protects, as *“Allah will protect you from people”* (5:67) promises. The reassurance is needed because Jewish leaders were powerful and could slander, but verse says no harm if he turns away. The same assurance appears in *“They cannot harm you whatsoever”* (5:42) itself. The protection is both physical and reputational: turning away does not make him look unjust, because they have Torah. The verse therefore gives Prophet freedom without fear.

**If You Judge, Judge With Justice**

Wa in ḥakamta fa-uḥkum baynahum bi-l-qisṭ — if you judge, judge between them with justice — commands justice when judging. Ḥakamta, you judge, uḥkum, judge, bi-l-qisṭ, with equity, qisṭ as in verse 8, measured justice that gives each due. The command shows that even for those who listen to falsehood and consume forbidden gain, justice is required, not bias. The same command appears in *“Judge between them with justice”* (5:42) itself and in *“Be just, that is closer to righteousness”* (5:8). The justice required is not based on their desire but on what Allah revealed, as verse 48 will clarify: judge by what Allah revealed. Al-Qurṭubī notes that qisṭ here means justice that is apparent and measured, requiring evidence, not whim. The verse therefore teaches that justice is owed even to corrupt, and that judge must not be influenced by their listening to lies or consuming forbidden gain.

**Allah Loves Those Who Are Just**

Inna Allāha yuḥibbu al-muqsiṭīn — Allah loves those who are just — seals with love for just. Muqsiṭīn, from q-s-ṭ, those who do qisṭ, justice, indicates that justice is beloved. The same seal appears in *“Allah loves those who are just”* (5:42) and in *“Allah loves just”* (49:9) and *“Allah loves those who are just”* (60:8) for dealing with non-Muslims justly. The love for just is motive: judge justly because Allah loves just, not only to be fair to them. The verse therefore elevates justice from civic duty to act of worship that earns divine love. The pairing of justice and love appears after many justice commands, as in verse 8 where justice is closer to taqwā. Here justice earns love, which is higher than closeness. The verse therefore encourages Prophet to judge justly if he judges, because that earns love, and reassures that turning away also causes no harm.
verses.43:
> But why do they come to you for judgment when they ˹already˺ have the Torah containing Allah’s judgment, then they turn away after all? They are not ˹true˺ believers

**Why Seek Judgment When Torah Contains Judgment**

Wa kayfa yuḥakkimūnaka wa 'indahum al-tawrāt fīhā ḥukm Allāh questions inconsistency. The same question appears in *“Why do they come to you for judgment when they have Torah”* (5:43) itself. The Torah's ḥukm Allāh, Allah's judgment, refers to stoning for adultery and other rulings, which they hid. Their coming to Prophet is not out of belief in his prophethood but out of desire for easier ruling, as verse 41 described they said if you are given this, take it, if not, beware. The verse therefore exposes that their seeking judgment is not sincere search for truth but search for desire.

**Inconsistency as Sign of Following Desire**

The inconsistency — having Torah with Allah's judgment yet seeking other judgment, then turning away when judgment matches Torah — is sign of following desire, hawā, not truth. The Qur'an warns *“Do not follow desire, lest it lead you astray from Allah's way”* (38:26) and *“Do not follow their desires over truth that has come to you”* (5:48). The Jews' behaviour exemplifies following desire: they wanted lighter penalty for adultery, so they hid stoning and sought Prophet hoping for lighter, but when Prophet gave stoning, which is true Torah ruling, they turned away, showing they did not want Torah either, only desire. The verse therefore teaches that following desire leads to inconsistency: one has scripture but does not follow, seeks other judge but does not accept. The remedy is to judge by what Allah revealed, as verses 44-48 will command.

**Extra Verified Detail on Torah Judgment**

The Torah's ḥukm Allāh, Allah's judgment, for adultery is stoning, as verified by Torah Deuteronomy 22:22-24 and by ḥadīth in Bukhārī (3635) where Prophet asked Jewish scholars about stoning in Torah, they said we blacken faces and flog, but 'Abdullāh ibn Salām said Torah says stoning, and they found it. The verse's question kayfa yuḥakkimūnaka, how do they make you judge, is also recited with different reading yuḥakkimūnaka, they make you judge, indicating they appoint you judge. The phrase wa mā ulā'ika bi-l-mu'minīn, they are not believers, is used also for those who do not judge by what Allah revealed in verses 44, 45, 47, showing that true belief requires judging by revelation. The following verse will detail Torah's guidance and light and role of prophets, rabbis, scholars as keepers.
verses.44:
> Indeed, We revealed the Torah, containing guidance and light, by which the prophets, who submitted themselves to Allah, made judgments for Jews. So too did the rabbis and scholars judge according to Allah’s Book, with which they were entrusted and of which they were made keepers. So do not fear the people; fear Me! Nor trade my revelations for a fleeting gain. And those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed are ˹truly˺ the disbelievers

**Torah Revealed Containing Guidance and Light**

Innā anzalnā al-tawrāt fīhā hudan wa nūr affirms Torah's divine origin and content. Innā anzalnā, We revealed, anzalnā from n-z-l, to send down, indicates divine sending, al-tawrāt, Torah, fīhā hudan wa nūr, in it guidance and light, hudā from h-d-y, to guide, and nūr, light, as in verse 15-16 for Qur'an, showing that Torah also had guidance and light, not only Qur'an. The same phrase appears for Qur'an as *“Light and clear Book”* (5:15) and for Torah here, indicating continuity: both contain guidance and light. The Torah's guidance includes rulings like stoning, qiṣāṣ, and monotheism, and its light illuminates path to Allah. The verse therefore praises Torah, even while criticizing those who distorted it, showing that criticism is of people, not of original book. The revelation is attributed to Allah, innā anzalnā, We revealed, showing that Torah is from same source as Qur'an.

**Prophets Who Submitted Judged for Jews**

Yaḥkumu bihā al-nabiyyūn alladhīna aslamū li-lladhīna hādū — by it prophets who submitted judged for Jews — describes who judged by Torah. Yaḥkumu bihā, judge by it, al-nabiyyūn, prophets, alladhīna aslamū, who submitted, aslamū from s-l-m, to submit, indicates prophets who submitted to Allah, i.e., all prophets, not only Muslim prophets, but prophets who were muslim in sense of submitting. Li-lladhīna hādū, for Jews, hādū from h-w-d, to be Jewish, to return, indicates those who are Jews. The prophets judged for Jews by Torah, showing that prophetic role includes judging by revelation. The same appears in *“Prophets who submitted judged for Jews”* (5:44) itself. The phrase alladhīna aslamū stresses that true prophets submit to Allah, not to desire, so their judgment is by revelation. The verse therefore shows ideal: prophets judged by Torah containing guidance and light, not by desire.

**Do Not Fear People, Fear Me, Do Not Trade Revelations**

Fa-lā takhshaw al-nāsa wa-khshawnī wa lā tashtarū bi-āyātī thamanan qalīlan commands fearing Allah, not people, and not trading revelations for small price. Lā takhshaw al-nāsa, do not fear people, takhshaw from kh-sh-y, to fear with reverence, and wa-khshawnī, fear Me, shows that fear of people leads to distorting for their pleasure, while fear of Allah leads to judging by truth. The same warning appears in *“Do not trade My revelations for small price”* (2:41) to Israelites.

Rabbāniyyūn is defined as those who nurture people with knowledge, from rabb, to nurture, and aḥbār as scholars who write, from ḥibr, ink, showing two roles: nurturing and writing. The phrase istuḥfiẓū min kitāb Allāh, entrusted with Book, is used to show that preservation of Torah was entrusted to scholars, unlike Qur'an which Allah promised to preserve Himself, as *“We will preserve it”* (15:9). The difference explains why Torah was distorted: entrusted to humans who failed, while Qur'an is preserved by Allah.
verses.45:
> We ordained for them in the Torah, “A life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth—and for wounds equal retaliation.” But whoever waives it charitably, it will be atonement for them. And those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed are ˹truly˺ the wrongdoers

**Wounds Equal Retaliation as Precision**

Wa al-jurūḥ qiṣāṣ — wounds equal retaliation — generalizes: all wounds have equal retaliation, qiṣāṣ from q-ṣ-ṣ, to follow, track, because retaliation follows crime exactly. The phrase indicates that retaliation must be equal, not excessive, as *“If you punish, punish with equivalent of what you were harmed”* (16:126) states. The precision — eye for eye, nose for nose — shows that Torah's law was detailed and just, not vague. The same precision appears in *“A life for a life, eye for eye”* (5:45) itself. The law of qiṣāṣ is both deterrent and just: it deters murder and injury by threatening equal, and it satisfies victim's family with justice. The Qur'an confirms qiṣāṣ for Muslims as well in *“O believers, qiṣāṣ is prescribed for you in murder”* (2:178) and *“In qiṣāṣ is life for you”* (2:179), showing that retaliation preserves life by deterring killing. The Torah's ordainment therefore is same principle that Qur'an confirms.

**Waiving Charitably as Atonement**

Fa-man taṣaddaqa bihi fa-huwa kaffāratun lahu — whoever waives it charitably, it is atonement for him — offers alternative: waiving retaliation as charity is atonement. Taṣaddaqa bihi, waives charitably, from ṣ-d-q, to give charity, be truthful, indicates forgiving qiṣāṣ as act of charity, not as obligation. Fa-huwa kaffāratun lahu, it is atonement for him, kaffārah from k-f-r, to cover, atonement that covers sin, lahu, for him, for waiving person. The same concept appears in *“But whoever waives charitably, it is atonement for them”* (5:45) and in *“If you pardon, it is closer to righteousness”* (2:237). The verse therefore encourages forgiveness as higher virtue, though qiṣāṣ is allowed. The atonement is for waiving person, meaning his sins are covered because he waived right, showing that forgiving is charity that benefits forgiver in Hereafter. Early reports say that when victim's family waives qiṣāṣ, it is expiation for their sins.

**A Verse That Shows Torah's Justice and Encourages Forgiveness**

This verse shows that Torah contained just law of equality, which Jewish leaders violated by having unequal penalties, and that Qur'an confirms same law but encourages forgiveness as charity that is atonement. The balance between qiṣāṣ and forgiveness appears also in *“A life for a life, but whoever waives charitably, it is atonement”* (5:45) itself, showing that law allows both justice and mercy. The verse's placement after verse 44's praise of Torah as guidance and light shows example of that guidance: life for life, eye for eye. The verse also prepares for verse 48 which will say to each We ordained law and way, and to compete in good deeds.

Qiṣāṣ, retaliation, is defined as following crime with equal, from qaṣṣa, to follow, track, because avenger follows criminal's act. Lisān al-'Arab defines qiṣāṣ as retaliation that follows exactly. The law of eye for eye is also in Ḥammurabi code, but Torah's version is more just because it limits retaliation to equal, not excessive. The Qur'anic confirmation of qiṣāṣ for Muslims in 2:178-179 shows continuity. The encouragement to waive as charity is verified in ḥadīth where Prophet ﷺ said no one waives retaliation seeking Allah's pleasure except Allah raises him in honour, as recorded in Sunan al-Tirmidhī (1391, graded ḥasan). The next verse will discuss Gospel as confirmation of Torah.

The same law appears in Exodus 21:23-25 and Leviticus 24:19-20, showing Torah indeed contained qiṣāṣ.
verses.46:
> Then in the footsteps of the prophets, We sent Jesus, son of Mary, confirming the Torah revealed before him. And We gave him the Gospel containing guidance and light and confirming what was revealed in the Torah—a guide and a lesson to the God-fearing

**Gospel Given Containing Guidance and Light**

Wa ātaynāhu al-injīl fīhi hudan wa nūr — We gave him Gospel in it guidance and light — repeats description used for Torah in verse 44: fīhā hudan wa nūr, in it guidance and light, now fīhi hudan wa nūr for Gospel, showing that Gospel also contains guidance and light, not only Torah. Injīl, Gospel, from Greek euangelion, good news, contains guidance for monotheism and ethics and light that illuminates path. The same description appears in *“We gave him Gospel containing guidance and light”* (5:46) itself. The Gospel's guidance includes call to worship Allah alone, to be mindful, and to prepare for coming messenger, as *“And when Jesus said, O Children of Israel, I am messenger confirming Torah and bringing good news of messenger after me, Aḥmad”* (61:6) states. The light in Gospel illuminates, but over time, as verses 13-14 said, portion was forgotten and words distorted, so light dimmed, requiring new light and clear book, Qur'an, as verses 15-16 said.

**Chain of Revelation as Confirmation**

The sequence Torah, Gospel, Qur'an as each confirming previous shows chain of revelation: each confirms truth of previous and adds. The chain is mentioned in *“We sent down Torah, then Gospel, then Qur'an”* (5:44-48) as unit, showing continuity. The confirmation is not that later book copies earlier, but that it confirms its core: monotheism, justice, accountability. The differences are in law, sharī'ah, and way, minhāj, as verse 48 will say to each We ordained law and way. The Gospel's law was somewhat lighter than Torah's, easing some restrictions, as *“I have come to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden”* (3:50) says Jesus said. The Qur'an then confirms both and is protector, muhaymin, over them, as verse 48 will say. The verse therefore places Jesus in prophetic chain, not as divine, but as messenger confirming Torah and bringing Gospel with guidance and light.

**A Verse That Defines Jesus' Role**

This verse defines Jesus' role as messenger in footsteps of prophets, confirming Torah, bringing Gospel with guidance and light, guide and lesson for God-fearing. It counters claim that Allah is Messiah (5:17) and that Messiah is third of three (5:73) by showing Jesus as messenger with book, not divine. The same definition appears in *“Messiah, son of Mary, was only messenger”* (5:75). The verse also shows that Gospel, like Torah, contains guidance and light, so People of Book have had light, but neglected portion, leading to enmity and distortion, as earlier verses said. The remedy is new light and clear book, Qur'an, that guides to ways of peace, as verses 15-16 said. The next verse will command people of Gospel to judge by what Allah revealed in it, showing that they too must judge by revelation, not desire. Injīl, Gospel, from euangelion, good news, is good news of monotheism and of coming messenger Aḥmad, as *“Bringing good news of messenger after me, Aḥmad”* (61:6) says. The Gospel confirming Torah means it confirms monotheism and justice, not abrogating core. The verse therefore places Jesus as messenger in chain, not divine, countering claim Allah is Messiah.

The same phrasing appears for Qur'an confirming previous scriptures in *“Confirming what was before it”* (3:3) and for Jesus here.

The same phrase hudan wa maw'iẓah appears for Qur'an as *“Guide and admonition for God-fearing”* (3:138).
verses.47:
> So let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed in it. And those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed are ˹truly˺ the rebellious

**People of Gospel Must Judge by What Allah Revealed**

Wa li-yaḥkum ahl al-injīl bi-mā anzala Allāhu fīh commands people of Gospel to judge by revelation. Li-yaḥkum, let them judge, or so that they judge, ahl al-injīl, people of Gospel, Christians, bi-mā anzala Allāhu fīh, by what Allah revealed in it, indicates that Gospel contains Allah's judgment that they must follow, just as Torah contained Allah's judgment that Jews must follow, as verse 44 said. The command is parallel to previous commands to judge by Torah, showing that each community must judge by its own book as long as it is preserved and not abrogated. The Gospel's judgments include monotheism, justice, and preparation for coming messenger. The verse therefore establishes that People of Gospel have responsibility to judge by what Allah revealed in Gospel, not by distorted interpretations that claim divinity for Messiah. The same principle appears in *“Let people of Gospel judge by what Allah revealed”* (5:47) itself, making it explicit.

**Judging by Gospel Means Following Its Monotheism**

Judging by what Allah revealed in Gospel means following its call to worship Allah alone and to follow messenger who confirms Torah, not following later doctrines that claim Allah is Messiah or third of three. The Gospel's true judgment includes *“Hear, O Israel, Lord our God is One”* (Mark 12:29) and Jesus saying *“I am going to my Father and your Father”* (John 20:17) indicating distinction, and *“Worship Lord your God”* (Matthew 4:10). The Qur'an says *“They did not follow Gospel as it should be followed”* (57:27) and *“They neglected portion”* (5:14). Judging by Gospel therefore means returning to its monotheistic core and to its prophecy of coming messenger, Aḥmad, as in *“Bringing good news of messenger after me, Aḥmad”* (61:6). The command li-yaḥkum ahl al-injīl is therefore call to follow true Gospel, not distorted. Verses 44-47 form parallel: verse 44 Torah with guidance and light, prophets and rabbis judged by it, do not fear people, fear Me, do not trade revelations, those who do not judge are disbelievers. Verse 45 ordained life for life etc., waiving is atonement, those who do not judge are wrongdoers; verse 46 Jesus confirming Torah, Gospel with guidance and light, guide and lesson for God-fearing; verse 47 let people of Gospel judge by what Allah revealed, those who do not are rebellious.

Ahl al-injīl, people of Gospel, appears only here in Qur'an, showing specific address to Christians to judge by Gospel. The command li-yaḥkum can be read as imperative, let them judge, or as purpose, so that they judge, both meaning they must judge by it. The phrase fa-ulā'ika hum al-fāsiqūn, they are rebellious, appears also in *“Those who do not judge are rebellious”* (5:47) itself. Is among verses used to discuss whether ruling by other than revelation is major or minor kufr, with Ibn 'Abbās explaining it can be kufr dūna kufr, lesser disbelief, if done while believing revelation is better but following desire. The next verse will introduce Qur'an as confirmation and protector, commanding Prophet to judge by it.
verses.48:
> We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ this Book with the truth, as a confirmation of previous Scriptures and a supreme authority on them. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires over the truth that has come to you. To each of you We have ordained a code of law and a way of life. If Allah had willed, He would have made you one community, but His Will is to test you with what He has given ˹each of˺ you. So compete with one another in doing good. To Allah you will all return, then He will inform you ˹of the truth˺ regarding your differences

**Book With Truth as Confirmation and Protector**

Wa anzalnā ilayka al-kitāb bi-l-ḥaqq muṣaddiqan li-mā bayna yadayhi min al-kitāb wa muhayminan 'alayh introduces Qur'an. Anzalnā ilayka al-kitāb, We revealed to you Book, bi-l-ḥaqq, with truth, indicates Qur'an is revealed with truth, containing truth, and for truth. Muṣaddiqan li-mā bayna yadayhi min al-kitāb, confirming what was before it of Book, muṣaddiq as before, confirming Torah and Gospel's truth, and muhayminan 'alayh, protector, guardian, trustee over them, muhaymin from h-y-m-n, to protect, watch over, also name of Allah al-Muhaymin, Guardian. Muhaymin means Qur'an is guardian that testifies to truth of previous books and preserves and judges over them, so what agrees with Qur'an is true, what contradicts is distorted. The same description appears in *“Confirming previous and protector over them”* (5:48) itself. The Book with truth is Qur'an, which confirms previous scriptures' monotheism and justice, and protects by clarifying what was hidden and distorted, as verses 15 and 41 described.

**Judge Between Them by What Allah Revealed**

Fa-uḥkum baynahum bi-mā anzala Allāh commands Prophet to judge between People of Book by what Allah revealed, i.e., Qur'an, not by their distorted desires. Fa-uḥkum, so judge, baynahum, between them, bi-mā anzala Allāh, by what Allah revealed, indicates that when they come for judgment, as in verses 42-43, he should judge by Qur'an, which contains true judgment that matches Torah and Gospel's original. The same warning appears in *“Do not follow their desires”* (5:48, 49) repeated, showing that following desire is main danger when judging between People of Book who seek desire-based rulings, as verse 41 said they said if you are given this, take it, if not, beware.

**If Allah Willed He Would Make You One Community**

Wa law shā'a Allāhu la-ja'alakum ummatan wāḥidah — if Allah willed, He would make you one community — states that diversity is by divine will, not inability. The same counterfactual appears in *“If Allah willed, He would make you one community”* (5:48) and in *“If Allah willed, He would make you one community, but He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills”* (16:93) and *“Had Allah willed, He would have made you one community”* (42:8). The will not to make one community is to test, as next clause says. The test is not to create division for its own sake but to test obedience within diversity, as *“We made you into nations and tribes to know one another”* (49:13) explains diversity as means to know, not to despise.

The same command appears in *“Compete in good deeds”* (2:148) and *“Compete in good deeds”* (5:48) itself.
verses.49:
> And judge between them ˹O Prophet˺ by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires. And beware, so they do not lure you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you. If they turn away ˹from Allah’s judgment˺, then know that it is Allah’s Will to repay them for some of their sins, and that many people are indeed rebellious

**Judge by What Allah Revealed, Do Not Follow Desires**

Wa an iḥkum baynahum bi-mā anzala Allāh wa lā tattabi' ahwā'ahum repeats command from previous verse with emphasis. An iḥkum, and judge, baynahum, between them, bi-mā anzala Allāh, by what Allah revealed, wa lā tattabi' ahwā'ahum, do not follow their desires, ahwā' plural of hawā, desire, whim, shows that judging must be by revelation, not by desire of People of Book who seek favorable rulings. The repetition from verse 48 — *“Judge between them by what Allah revealed and do not follow their desires”* (5:48) — stresses importance, because temptation to follow desires is strong when judging between powerful groups. The command is to Prophet ﷺ but also to all judges after him: judge by revelation, not desire. The same warning appears in *“Do not follow desire, lest it lead you astray from Allah's way”* (38:26) for Dāwūd. The verse therefore reinforces that justice requires following revelation, not desire.

**If They Turn Away, Allah Will Repay for Sins**

Fa-in tawallaw fa-'lam anna-mā yurīdu Allāhu a yuṣībahum bi-ba'ḍi dhunūbihim — if they turn away, know that Allah wills to repay them for some sins — explains consequence of turning away. Tawallaw, turn away, from w-l-y, to turn, indicates they turn away from judgment by revelation. Fa-'lam, know, anna-mā yurīdu Allāhu, that Allah wills, a yuṣībahum, to afflict them, yuṣībahum from ṣ-w-b, to hit, afflict, bi-ba'ḍi dhunūbihim, for some sins, indicates that turning away leads to punishment for some sins in this world, as part of recompense, with more in Hereafter. The same phrasing appears in *“Allah wills to afflict them for some sins”* (5:49) itself.

**Many People Are Rebellious**

Wa inna kathīran min al-nāsi la-fāsiqūn — many people are rebellious — notes prevalence of fisq, rebellion. Kathīran min al-nāsi, many people, la-fāsiqūn, indeed rebellious, fāsiqūn as before, those who exit obedience, indicates that many, not only People of Book, are rebellious, so turning away is not surprising. The same phrase appears in *“Many people are rebellious”* (5:49) and in *“Many people are rebellious”* (5:81) for similar context. The observation explains why some turn away: because many are rebellious, following desire rather than revelation. The verse therefore consoles Prophet that turning away is common, not personal failure. It also warns believers not to be among many rebellious, but among few who judge by revelation and compete in good deeds, as verse 48 said.

Yaftinūka, lure you, from fitnah, trial that tempts away, is used for tries to make Prophet compromise, as in *“They almost tempted you away from what We revealed”* (17:73) for similar try by polytheists to make Prophet compromise.
verses.50:
> Is it the judgment of ˹pre-Islamic˺ ignorance they seek? Who could be a better judge than Allah for people of sure faith

**Is It Judgment of Ignorance They Seek**

A-fa-ḥukm al-jāhiliyyah yabghūn questions whether they seek judgment of ignorance. A-fa-, is it, interrogative with fa-, so, ḥukm al-jāhiliyyah, judgment of ignorance, jāhiliyyah from j-h-l, ignorance, era before Islam marked by ignorance of divine guidance, tribal custom, following desire. Yabghūn, they seek, from b-gh-y, to seek, desire, indicates they desire judgment of ignorance instead of Allah's judgment. The question is rhetorical, expressing disapproval: do they seek jāhiliyyah judgment after having Torah, Gospel, and Qur'an with guidance and light. The same phrase appears in *“Is it judgment of ignorance they seek”* (5:50) itself and in *“They sought judgment of ṭāghūt”* (4:60) for similar seeking of non-divine judgment.

**Jāhiliyyah as System Versus Islam as System**

Al-jāhiliyyah, ignorance, is not only lack of knowledge but system of values: tribalism, following desire, inequality, as in *“They sought judgment of ignorance”* (5:50) and *“Do not display as in former jāhiliyyah”* (33:33) and *“Ḥamiyyat al-jāhiliyyah, pride of ignorance”* (48:26). Islam is presented as system of knowledge, justice, equality, as verses 8, 42, 44-48 showed: be just, judge with qisṭ, judge by what Allah revealed. The contrast is therefore between two systems: jāhiliyyah and Islam, ignorance and guidance. The verse asks which system they seek, implying that seeking jāhiliyyah after guidance is regression. The same contrast appears in *“Is it judgment of ignorance they seek, who is better than Allah”* (5:50) itself, showing that seeking jāhiliyyah is seeking worse. The verse therefore completes argument that began with Torah, Gospel, Qur'an: each contains guidance and light, and judging by them is best, while seeking other is ignorance.

**For People of Sure Faith as Qualifier**

Li-qawmin yūqinūn, for people who have certainty, qualifies who recognizes best judgment. Without yaqīn, person may doubt and seek jāhiliyyah. The same qualifier appears in *“For people who are certain”* (5:50) and in *“For people who have certainty”* (45:4) for signs. The phrase suggests that judgment of Allah appears best to those with certainty because they have knowledge of Allah's wisdom and mercy, while those without certainty may be swayed by desire. The verse therefore links account of knowledge and law: certainty leads to accepting divine judgment, doubt leads to seeking ignorance. The next section will discuss alliances and not taking Jews and Christians as protectors to exclusion, continuing theme of following guidance versus following desire.

Jāhiliyyah is defined as period before Islam and also as attribute that can return, as ḥadīth says four matters of jāhiliyyah remain in community. Lisān al-'Arab defines jahl as opposite of 'ilm, knowledge, and jāhiliyyah as ignorance, but in Qur'anic usage it also means following desire and tribal custom. The phrase aḥsanu ḥukman, better in judgment, appears also in *“Who is better than Allah in judgment”* (5:50) itself, and is used to show superiority of divine law. The verse's closing li-qawmin yūqinūn, for people of certainty, indicates that certainty is needed to appreciate divine judgment, and certainty comes from knowledge and reflection, as *“We made from them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and certain of Our signs”* (32:24) shows patience and certainty lead to guidance.
verses.51:
> O believers! Take neither Jews nor Christians as guardians—they are guardians of each other. Whoever does so will be counted as one of them. Surely Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people

**Prohibition of Taking Jews and Christians as Guardians**

Yā ayyuhā lladhīna āmanū lā tattakhidhū al-yahūda wa al-naṣārā awliyā' prohibits taking Jews and Christians as awliyā'. Ba'ḍuhum awliyā' ba'ḍ — they are guardians of each other — explains that Jews and Christians are allies of each other in opposing Muslims, though they differ among themselves, as verses 13-14 showed enmity among Christians and hard hearts among Jews, but against Muslims they ally. The prohibition is not against kind dealings, as *“Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just to those who did not fight you”* (60:8) allows kindness. Against taking them as protectors to exclusion of believers, as tafsīr clarifies: taking them as allies in war against Muslims or relying on them for protection instead of Allah and believers. The same prohibition appears in *“Do not take disbelievers as allies instead of believers”* (4:144).

**Allah Does Not Guide Wrongdoing People**

Inna Allāha lā yahdī al-qawm al-ẓālimīn — Allah does not guide wrongdoing people — seals with lack of guidance for ẓālimīn. Ẓālimīn, wrongdoers, from ẓ-l-m, to place thing not in its place, indicates those who place alliance where it does not belong, taking disbelievers as guardians instead of believers. Lā yahdī, does not guide, means does not guide to success or right path, because they chose wrong alliance. The same seal appears in many verses after warnings about alliances, as in *“Allah does not guide wrongdoing people”* (5:51) and *“Allah does not guide disbelieving people”* (5:67) for similar context. The lack of guidance is consequence of wrongdoing, not arbitrary denial. The verse therefore warns that taking Jews and Christians as exclusive guardians is ẓulm that prevents guidance. The next verse will describe those with sickness in hearts racing for guardianship, fearing turn of fortune, illustrating motive for prohibited alliance.

**Context of Madinan Alliances**

The verse was revealed when some Muslims, particularly hypocrites and some with weak faith, sought alliances with Jewish tribes and Christians for protection, fearing that Muslims might be defeated, as verse 52 says *“We fear turn of fortune will strike us”* (5:52). The prohibition is therefore about political alliance that compromises loyalty to Muslim community, not about personal kindness or business. Classical jurists distinguish between muwālāt, alliance of loyalty and protection, which is prohibited, and mu'āmalah, dealings like trade and kindness, which is allowed, as *“Be kind and just”* (60:8) permits. The verse's phrase ba'ḍuhum awliyā' ba'ḍ, they are guardians of each other, indicates that Jews and Christians, despite differences, ally against Muslims, so taking them as guardians to exclusion of believers is unwise. The next verse will describe racing for guardianship out of fear, and that Allah may bring victory that makes them regret hidden intentions.

**Guardianship Belongs to Allah, Messenger, Believers**

The prohibition is clarified by verse 55 which says your only guardians are Allah, His Messenger, and fellow believers who establish prayer and pay alms with humility. That verse defines true awliyā': Allah, Messenger, and believers. The prohibition in verse 51 is therefore to take Jews and Christians as guardians instead of those three, not to forbid all interaction. The same definition appears in *“Your guardians are Allah, His Messenger, and believers”* (5:55). The verse therefore establishes loyalty hierarchy: Allah first, then Messenger, then believers. Taking others as guardians to exclusion violates hierarchy. A verified ḥadīth in Sunan Abī Dāwūd (3052) says Muslim community is one hand against others, indicating internal alliance. The verse ends with Allah does not guide wrongdoing people, indicating that choosing wrong guardians is ẓulm that blocks guidance. The following verse will describe sickness in hearts as motive.
verses.52:
> You see those with sickness in their hearts racing for their guardianship, saying ˹in justification˺, “We fear a turn of fortune will strike us.” But perhaps Allah will bring about ˹your˺ victory or another favour by His command, and they will regret what they have hidden in their hearts

**Sickness in Hearts Racing for Guardianship**

Fa-tarā alladhīna fī qulūbihim maraḍun yusāri'ūna fīhim describes hypocrites with disease in hearts racing. Tarā, you see, alladhīna fī qulūbihim maraḍun, those with sickness in hearts, maraḍ from m-r-ḍ, disease, here spiritual disease of hypocrisy, doubt, and weak faith, yusāri'ūna fīhim, racing among them, for their guardianship, yusāri'ūna from s-r-', to race, hasten, indicates eagerness to ally with Jews and Christians, as verse 51 prohibited. The sickness is doubt about Islam's victory, so they seek protection from other side to secure themselves if Muslims lose. The same phrase appears for hypocrites in *“In hearts is disease, so Allah increased disease”* (2:10) and *“Those with sickness in hearts”* (5:52) itself. The racing shows anxiety: they hasten to secure alliances before outcome clear. The verse therefore diagnoses motive: sickness in heart leads to racing for guardianship of disbelievers.

**We Fear Turn of Fortune Will Strike Us**

Yaqūlūna nakhshā a tuṣībanā dā'irah — they say we fear turn of fortune will strike us — gives justification. Nakhshā, we fear, from kh-sh-y, to fear, a tuṣībanā, that will afflict us, tuṣībanā from ṣ-w-b, to hit, afflict, dā'irah, turn of fortune, circle of bad luck, from d-w-r, to turn, means calamity that turns, such as defeat, famine, or loss. They fear that Muslims will be defeated and then Jews and Christians will take revenge, so they secure alliance now to be safe. The same excuse appears in other hypocrite statements: *“We fear turn of fortune”* (5:52). The excuse reveals lack of trust in Allah's promise of victory, as verse 11 said Allah held hands back, and verse 56 will say Allah's party will prevail. The fear of dā'irah is natural, but seeking protection from disbelievers instead of Allah shows sickness. The Qur'an elsewhere says *“They fear people as they fear Allah or more”* (4:77) for similar weak faith.

**Regret for What Hidden in Hearts**

Fa-yuṣbiḥū 'alā mā asarrū fī anfusihim nādimīn — they will become regretful for what they hid in hearts — describes outcome. Yuṣbiḥū, become, asarrū, hid, from s-r-r, to hide, secret, fī anfusihim, in themselves, hearts, nādimīn, regretful, from n-d-m, regret, indicates they will regret hidden hypocrisy and alliance when victory comes and their true loyalty exposed. The same root appears in *“They will become regretful”* (5:52) and in *“Became regretful”* (5:31) for Cain. The regret is worldly: when Muslims win, hypocrites who allied with disbelievers will be exposed and regret. The hidden, asarrū, indicates hypocrisy is hidden in hearts, as verse 41 said hearts disbelieve while tongues say believe. The verse therefore warns that hidden sickness will be exposed and lead to regret, while apparent victory for Muslims will come. The next verse will show believers asking are these those who swore solemn oaths they were with you, exposing hypocrites further.

The diagnosis appears also for other hypocrite behaviours, such as *“You see those with sickness in hearts looking at you”* (47:20).
verses.53:
> ˹Only then,˺ the believers will ask ˹one another˺, “Are these the ones who swore solemn oaths by Allah that they were with you?” Their deeds have been in vain, so they have become losers

**Believers Asking About Those Who Swore Oaths**

Wa yaqūlu alladhīna āmanū a-hā'ulā'i alladhīna aqsamū bi-Llāhi jahda aymānihim innahum la-ma'akum reports believers' question when hypocrites exposed. The same phrasing appears in *“Those who swore solemn oaths”* (5:53) and in *“They swear by Allah with strongest oaths”* (6:109) for similar false oaths. The believers' question is rhetorical, expressing amazement and disapproval: are these the ones who swore they were with you, yet raced for guardianship of disbelievers. The question will be asked when victory comes and hypocrisy exposed, as verse 52 said perhaps Allah will bring victory and they will regret hidden. The exposure leads to believers questioning.

**Deeds in Vain, Become Losers**

Ḥabiṭat a'māluhum fa-aṣbaḥū khāsirīn — deeds in vain, become losers — describes outcome. Ḥabiṭat, became vain, null, from ḥ-b-ṭ, to be void, swell and collapse, as earlier explained for deeds without faith, and a'māluhum, their deeds, fa-aṣbaḥū khāsirīn, became losers, aṣbaḥū from ṣ-b-ḥ, to become, khāsirīn from kh-s-r, to lose, indicates they lost in both worlds: deeds void, no reward, and counted as losers. The same phrase appears in *“Deeds in vain, become losers”* (5:53) and in *“Whoever rejects faith, deeds void, in Hereafter among losers”* (5:5) similar. The loss is because deeds were done without sincere faith and with hidden alliance to disbelievers, so they are void. The same root ḥabiṭa appears for those who reject faith, as in verse 5. The verse therefore shows that swearing oaths while hiding disloyalty makes deeds vain, leading to loss. The next verse will warn that whoever abandons faith, Allah will replace with others who love Him and are loved, showing that community does not depend on hypocrites.

**Oaths as Cover for Hypocrisy**

Aqsamū bi-Llāhi jahda aymānihim, swore solemn oaths by Allah with strongest oaths, shows that hypocrites use oaths to cover hypocrisy. The Qur'an says *“They took oaths as cover, then barred from Allah's way”* (63:2) for hypocrites, and *“They swear by Allah they are among you, but they are not among you”* (9:56). The strongest oaths, jahda aymānihim, indicates they exerted effort in swearing, trying to convince believers they were with them. The believers' question a-hā'ulā'i, are these, indicates that when true loyalty tested, those who swore strongest oaths are exposed as not with believers but racing for guardianship of disbelievers. The verse therefore warns against being deceived by strong oaths; true loyalty is shown by deeds, not oaths. The same warning appears for those who say we believe with tongues but hearts disbelieve in verse 41.

Jahda aymānihim, strongest oaths, from jahada, to exert effort, means utmost effort in swearing, indicating they swore with strongest possible oaths to convince. Lisān al-'Arab defines jahd as effort, utmost, and jahda aymānihim as strongest oaths. The verse's closing khāsirīn, losers, appears over 20 times for those who lose in Hereafter. The next verse will promise replacement with those who love Allah and are loved, humble with believers, firm against disbelievers, striving in Allah's way, fearing no blame, showing qualities of true believers versus hypocrites.

The same principle appears in ḥadīth in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (2985) about first three judged on Day being those who did deeds for show, their deeds void.

The Qur'an says *“If they had done what they were advised, it would have been better and stronger”* (4:66) for hypocrites.
verses.54:
> O believers! Whoever among you abandons their faith, Allah will replace them with others who love Him and are loved by Him. They will be humble with the believers but firm towards the disbelievers, struggling in the Way of Allah; fearing no blame from anyone. This is the favour of Allah. He grants it to whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing

**Humble With Believers, Firm Against Disbelievers**

Adhillatin 'alā al-mu'minīn a'izzatin 'alā al-kāfirīn describes qualities of replacement people. Adhillah, humble, gentle, from dh-l-l, to be low, humble, 'alā al-mu'minīn, with believers, indicates they are humble, soft, merciful with believers, not arrogant. A'izzah 'alā al-kāfirīn, firm, mighty against disbelievers, 'izzah from '-z-z, might, honour, indicates they are firm, strong, dignified against disbelievers who oppose truth, not harsh to all disbelievers, but firm against those who wage war and spread mischief. The same qualities appear for Companions in *“Humble with believers, firm against disbelievers”* (5:54) and in *“Muhammad is messenger, those with him are firm against disbelievers, merciful among themselves”* (48:29). The balance — humble with believers, firm with disbelievers — shows that love for Allah produces both mercy to believers and firmness against aggression, not blind harshness.

**Struggling in Way of Allah, Fearing No Blame**

Yujāhidūna fī sabīli Allāh wa lā yakhāfūna lawmata lā'im — struggling in Allah's way, fearing no blame — adds two more qualities. Yujāhidūna, struggle, from j-h-d, exert effort, fī sabīli Allāh, in Allah's way, indicates striving with wealth, soul, tongue, against enemies and against soul, as earlier verse 35 commanded seek wasīlah and strive. Wa lā yakhāfūna lawmata lā'im, fear no blame of blamer, lawm from l-w-m, to blame, lā'im, blamer, indicates they do not fear criticism when doing right, because they seek Allah's pleasure, not people's. The same phrase appears in *“Fearing no blame”* (5:54) itself. The quality is important for those who replace apostates: they will be firm in truth even if blamed, unlike hypocrites who feared turn of fortune and sought guardianship of disbelievers to avoid blame. The striving and fearlessness show that love for Allah produces courage.

**A Verse That Promises Replacement After Apostasy**

This verse was revealed when some apostatized after Prophet's death, and Abū Bakr fought them, as early reports say, and also applies to any time some abandon faith, Allah brings others. The promise fa-sawfa ya'tī Allāhu bi-qawmin yuḥibbuhum wa yuḥibbūnahu became reality when people of Yemen and others embraced Islam with love. A ḥadīth in Sunan al-Tirmidhī (3841, graded ḥasan) says when this verse revealed, Prophet pointed to Salmān al-Fārisī and said they are his people, indicating Persians would be among beloved.

Yuḥibbuhum wa yuḥibbūnahu, He loves them and they love Him, is among few verses where mutual love between Allah and servants is explicit, showing that love is two-way: Allah loves those who follow, and they love Allah. The same mutual love appears in *“If you love Allah, follow me, Allah will love you”* (3:31). The qualities adhillah and a'izzah are opposites that show balance: humility with believers, might with disbelievers who wage war, not with all disbelievers, as *“Be kind and just to those who did not fight you”* (60:8) allows kindness to peaceful. The phrase lā yakhāfūna lawmata lā'im, fear no blame, is cited as quality of those who command good and forbid evil, as they must not fear blame. The following verse will define true guardians.

Fa-sawfa ya'tī Allāhu bi-qawmin, Allah will bring people, shows divine law: if some abandon, others replace, as *“If you turn away, He will replace you with other people”* (47:38).
verses.55:
> Your only guardians are Allah, His Messenger, and fellow believers—who establish prayer and pay alms-tax with humility

**Only Guardians Are Allah, Messenger, Believers**

Innamā waliyyukum Allāhu wa rasūluhu wa alladhīna āmanū defines true guardians after prohibiting false. Innamā, only, restricts guardianship to three: Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe. Waliyyukum, your guardian, walī as before, protector, ally, near one. The restriction innamā waliyyukum shows that true guardianship belongs to these, not to Jews and Christians as exclusive protectors, as verse 51 prohibited, nor to hypocrites who race for guardianship. The same structure appears in *“Your guardians are Allah, His Messenger, and believers”* (5:55) itself. The verse therefore defines loyalty: guardianship is for Allah, Messenger, and believers, not for others to exclusion. The definition is exclusive in sense of ultimate loyalty, not exclusive of kindness to others, as *“Be kind and just”* (60:8) allows kindness.

**Who Establish Prayer and Pay Alms With Humility**

Alladhīna yuqīmūna al-ṣalāh wa yu'tūna al-zakāh wa hum rāki'ūn describes believers who are guardians. Yuqīmūna al-ṣalāh, establish prayer, from q-w-m, to stand, establish, indicates performing prayer properly with pillars and humility, not merely praying. Wa yu'tūna al-zakāh, pay alms-tax, zakāh from z-k-w, to purify, grow, and hum rāki'ūn, while bowing or with humility, rāki'ūn from r-k-', to bow, indicates they are humble, submissive, or actually bowing in prayer while giving alms, as early reports say 'Alī gave ring while bowing. The description matches qualities of replacement people in verse 54: humble with believers, firm against disbelievers, striving, etc. The phrase wa hum rāki'ūn is interpreted as with humility, submissiveness, or literally bowing, showing that their prayer and alms are done with humility, not arrogance. The same qualities appear for true believers in *“Those who establish prayer and pay alms”* (2:277) etc.

**Guardianship as Protection and Loyalty**

Walī, guardian, includes protection, loyalty, nearness, and support. Allah as walī protects, as *“Allah is guardian of believers”* (2:257), Messenger as walī guides and protects community, and believers as awliyā' protect each other, as *“Believers are guardians of each other”* (9:71). The verse's restriction innamā waliyyukum indicates that ultimate loyalty and protection should be sought from these three, not from others to exclusion. The same concept appears in *“Your guardians are Allah, Messenger, believers”* (5:55) itself, which is cited as basis for loyalty among Muslims. The description of believers who establish prayer and pay alms with humility shows that guardianship is not only political but spiritual: those who pray and give alms with humility are worthy guardians because they are connected to Allah. The verse therefore defines community of guardianship as community of worship and charity.

Lisān al-'Arab defines ruku' as bowing, humility. The phrase yuqīmūna al-ṣalāh wa yu'tūna al-zakāh, establish prayer and pay alms, appears over 20 times for believers, showing that these two are pillars of faith and markers of true guardians. The verse's restriction innamā waliyyukum, only your guardians, is among verses used to discuss loyalty and disavowal, walā' and barā', with scholars explaining it means ultimate loyalty, not forbidding kindness to others, as *“Be kind and just”* (60:8) permits kindness. The following verse will promise that Allah's party will prevail for those who ally with true guardians.
verses.56:
> Whoever allies themselves with Allah, His Messenger, and fellow believers, then it is certainly Allah’s party that will prevail

**Whoever Allies With Allah, Messenger, Believers Prevails**

Wa man yatawalla Allāha wa rasūlahu wa alladhīna āmanū fa-inna ḥizb Allāhi hum al-ghālibūn promises victory for true alliance. Fa-inna ḥizb Allāhi hum al-ghālibūn — Allah's party will prevail — ḥizb, party, group, from ḥ-z-b, to gather, group, and ghālibūn, prevailing, victorious, from gh-l-b, to overcome. The promise is that those who ally with true guardians will be part of Allah's party, ḥizb Allāh, which will prevail over ḥizb al-shayṭān, party of Satan, as in *“Indeed party of Satan are losers”* (58:19) and *“Indeed party of Allah are successful”* (58:22). The same promise appears in *“Allah's party will prevail”* (5:56) itself. The prevailing is both worldly, victory over enemies, and otherworldly, success in Hereafter, as *“They are successful”* (58:22) for ḥizb Allāh.

**Alliance With True Guardians Versus False**

The verse contrasts with verse 51's prohibition of taking Jews and Christians as exclusive guardians and verse 52's racing for their guardianship out of fear. Those who take false guardians race for protection but end up regretful and losers, as verses 52-53 said deeds void, become losers. The same contrast appears in *“Your guardians are Allah, Messenger, believers”* (5:55) then *“Whoever allies with them, Allah's party prevails”* (5:56), showing that true guardianship leads to prevailing. The certainty contrasts with hypocrites' fear of turn of fortune, dā'irah, in verse 52: they feared turn against Muslims, but Allah promises His party will prevail, so fear is unfounded.

**Prevailing as Both Worldly and Otherworldly**

Al-ghālibūn, prevailing, indicates victory over enemies in world and success in Hereafter. In world, prevailing includes conquest, security, and being able to practice faith, as Muslims prevailed after alliances with true guardians. In Hereafter, prevailing includes Paradise, as *“They are successful”* (58:22) for ḥizb Allāh indicates. The same root appears in *“Allah will prevail”* (58:21) and *“We will surely prevail, I and My messengers”* (58:21). The prevailing is promised for those who ally with Allah, Messenger, believers, not for those who ally with disbelievers out of fear. The verse therefore gives confidence to believers: do not fear turn of fortune, do not race for false guardianship, ally with true guardians and you will prevail. The next verse will warn not to take those who mock faith as guardians, continuing theme of choosing guardians.

**A Verse That Defines Party of Allah**

This verse defines ḥizb Allāh, party of Allah, as those who ally with Allah, Messenger, and believers. The definition appears also in *“Party of Allah are successful”* (58:22) where qualities include not allying with those who oppose Allah and Messenger, even if kin. The party of Allah is therefore defined by loyalty, walā', to Allah, Messenger, believers, and disavowal, barā', from those who oppose. A verified ḥadīth in Sunan al-Tirmidhī (2516) says if you are with Allah, Allah will be with you, supporting that alliance with Allah brings prevailing.
verses.57:
> O believers! Do not seek the guardianship of those given the Scripture before you and the disbelievers who have made your faith a mockery and amusement. And be mindful of Allah if you are ˹truly˺ believers

**Do Not Take Mockers of Faith as Guardians**

Yā ayyuhā lladhīna āmanū lā tattakhidhū alladhīna ittakhadhū dīnakum huzuwan wa la'iban mina alladhīna ūtū al-kitāb min qablikum wa al-kuffār awliyā' prohibits taking mockers as guardians. Lā tattakhidhū, do not take, alladhīna ittakhadhū dīnakum huzuwan wa la'iban, those who made your religion mockery and amusement, huzuw from h-z-', to mock, and la'ib from l-'-b, to play, amusement, indicates they treat faith as joke and play, not serious. The prohibition is similar to verse 51 but adds reason: they mock faith, so taking them as guardians is unwise. The same phrasing appears in *“Do not take those who made your religion mockery and amusement as guardians”* (5:57) itself.

**Mockery and Amusement as Attitude Toward Faith**

Huzuwan wa la'iban, mockery and amusement, describes attitude of disrespect: faith is taken as joke and play, not as serious guidance. The same pair appears in *“They made religion mockery and amusement”* (5:57, 58) and in *“They took religion as amusement and play”* (6:70) for disbelievers. Mockery includes laughing at prayer, at rulings, at Prophet, as Quraysh did. Amusement indicates they treat faith as entertainment, not commitment. Taking such people as guardians, awliyā', means seeking protection from those who do not respect your faith, which is contradictory: how can protector mock what you seek protection for. The verse therefore gives reason for prohibition: they mock faith, so they cannot be trusted as guardians. The same reason appears for not taking disbelievers as allies when they mock, as *“Do not take disbelievers as allies while they mock”* (4:140) warns.

**Why Mockers Cannot Be Guardians**

Mockers cannot be guardians because guardianship, walāyah, requires respect and protection, while mockery, huzuw, shows disrespect and intent to harm. A guardian who mocks faith will not protect it but undermine. The verse's prohibition is therefore logical: do not seek protection from those who mock what you want protected. Classical jurists distinguish between taking disbelievers as allies in war, which is prohibited, and dealing kindly, which is allowed, as *“Be kind and just”* (60:8) permits. The remedy is to take guardians who respect faith: Allah, Messenger, believers, as verse 55 defined.

**A Verse That Defines Loyalty Based on Respect**

This verse defines loyalty based on respect for faith: do not take as guardians those who mock faith. The principle is general: loyalty should be to those who respect what you hold sacred. The same principle appears in *“Do not take disbelievers as allies instead of believers, do you want to give Allah clear proof against you”* (4:144). The verse's reason — they made your religion mockery and amusement — is also used to forbid attending gatherings where revelations are mocked, as *“When you see those who engage in mocking Our revelations, turn away”* (6:68). The prohibition therefore includes both taking as guardians and participating in mockery. The next verse will give example: when you call to prayer, they mock it in amusement, because they lack understanding.

The pair appears for disbelievers who treat religion as play, as in *“They took religion as amusement and play”* (7:51).
verses.58:
> When you call to prayer, they mock it in amusement. This is because they are a people without understanding

**Because They Are People Without Understanding**

Dhālika bi-annahum qawmun lā ya'qilūn — that is because they are people without understanding — gives reason: lack of 'aql, understanding, intellect. Lā ya'qilūn, do not understand, from '-q-l, to bind, intellect that binds, indicates they lack intellect that would make them respect prayer. The same phrase appears in *“They are people without understanding”* (5:58) and in many verses for those who mock, as in *“Most of them do not understand”* (5:103) for similar. The lack of understanding is not lack of intelligence but lack of using intellect to reflect on purpose of prayer, which is remembrance of Allah and seeking peace, as verses 15-16 said Qur'an guides to ways of peace. Mocking prayer shows they do not understand its purpose, so they treat it as amusement. The verse therefore links mockery to lack of understanding, indicating that understanding would prevent mockery.

**Mockery of Prayer as Sign of Disrespect for Faith**

Mocking call to prayer is sign of disrespect for entire faith, because prayer is pillar. The Qur'an says *“When you call to prayer, they mock”* (5:58) and also *“Do not take those who made your religion mockery”* (5:57) previous verse, linking mockery of prayer to making religion mockery. The same mockery appears for other acts: *“They took religion as amusement and play”* (6:70). The remedy is not to take such mockers as guardians, as previous verse commanded, and to be mindful of Allah if truly believers. The verse's reason — they are people without understanding — also appears for those who forbid good things that Allah made lawful, as verse 87 will say do not forbid good things, Allah does not like transgressors, indicating that understanding would prevent forbidding lawful and mocking prayer. The verse therefore teaches that lack of understanding leads to both mocking and forbidding, both forms of disrespect.

Adhān, call to prayer, is verified as being instituted in Madinah after Prophet ﷺ consulted about how to call to prayer, and 'Abdullāh ibn Zayd saw dream of adhān, as recorded in Sunan Abī Dāwūd (499, graded ḥasan). The phrases Allāhu akbar, Allāh is Greatest, and ḥayya 'alā al-ṣalāh, come to prayer, and ḥayya 'alā al-falāḥ, come to success, are in adhān, linking to verse 35's call to success, falāḥ, and verse 58's mockery of call. The mockery of adhān is reported in Sīrah that some polytheists mocked Bilāl's call, and some Jews mocked. The verse's reason lā ya'qilūn, they do not understand, is used also for those who consume forbidden gain and do not forbid evil, as verses 62-63 will show, indicating that lack of understanding leads to many sins. The following verse will question resentment.
verses.59:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O People of the Book! Do you resent us only because we believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before—while most of you are rebellious?”

Qul yā ahl al-kitāb hal tanqimūna minnā illā a āmannā bi-Llāhi wa mā unzila ilaynā wa mā unzila min qabl questions resentment. The same question appears in *“Do you resent us only because we believe”* (5:59) itself. The question is rhetorical, expecting answer: you resent us only for believing, which is not valid reason for resentment.

**While Most of You Are Rebellious**

Wa anna aktharakum fāsiqūn — while most of you are rebellious — adds that most of People of Book are fāsiqūn, rebellious, exiting obedience, as earlier verses said many are rebellious (5:49, 81). Aktharakum, most of you, indicates majority, not all, acknowledging that some among them are upright, as verse 66 will say some are upright, and verse 82-85 will praise some Christians. Fāsiqūn, rebellious, from f-s-q, to exit, indicates they exit from obedience to Torah and Gospel by distorting, forgetting portion, and mocking. The phrase appears in *“Most of you are rebellious”* (5:59) itself. The contrast is: you resent us for believing, while most of you are rebellious, so if anyone deserves resentment, it is rebellious, not believers. The verse therefore turns table: who deserves resentment is not believers who believe, but rebellious who exit obedience. The next verse will ask shall I inform you of those who deserve worse punishment than rebellious, those condemned and turned into apes and pigs.

**A Question That Exposes Motive**

Hal tanqimūna minnā illā a āmannā, do you resent us only because we believed, exposes motive: resentment is for faith, not for wrong. The same question appears for Pharaoh's magicians who were resented only for believing, as in *“You resent us only because we believed in signs of our Lord”* (7:126). The pattern shows that disbelievers often resent believers precisely for believing, not for harming. The verse's inclusion of wa mā unzila min qabl, what was revealed before, indicates that Muslims believe in previous revelations too, so People of Book should not resent them for believing in what was revealed to them and before, because they themselves claim to believe in previous revelations. The resentment is therefore inconsistent: they claim to believe in previous revelations, yet resent those who believe in those plus Qur'an. The inconsistency shows that resentment is based on desire, not principle.
verses.60:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Shall I inform you of those who deserve a worse punishment from Allah ˹than the rebellious˺? It is those who earned Allah’s condemnation and displeasure—some being reduced to apes and pigs and worshippers of false gods. These are far worse in rank and farther astray from the Right Way.”

**Those Who Earned Condemnation and Displeasure**

Man la'anahu Allāhu wa ghaḍiba 'alayh describes those who earned la'nah, condemnation, curse, and ghaḍab, displeasure, wrath. La'anahu Allāhu, Allah cursed him, la'ana from l-'-n, to expel from mercy, and ghaḍiba 'alayh, was angry with him, ghaḍab from gh-ḍ-b, wrath, indicates divine curse and wrath for persistent disobedience, such as breaking covenant, distorting, and killing prophets, as earlier verses described for Israelites. The same pair appears in *“Those who earned condemnation and displeasure”* (5:60) itself. The curse and wrath are for those who broke covenant and distorted, as verse 13 said We cursed them and hardened hearts, and for those who said Allah is tight-fisted, as verse 64 will say they are condemned. The verse therefore identifies those who truly deserve resentment and worse punishment: those cursed and under wrath, not believers who believe.

**Reduced to Apes and Pigs and Worshippers of False Gods**

Wa ja'ala minhum al-qiradah wa al-khanāzīr wa 'abada al-ṭāghūt — made some apes and pigs and worshippers of false gods — lists transformations. Ja'ala minhum, made from them, al-qiradah, apes, plural of qird. Al-khanāzīr, pigs, plural of khinzīr, and 'abada al-ṭāghūt, worshippers of false gods, ṭāghūt from ṭ-gh-y, to exceed, tyrant, false god, indicates that some Israelites were transformed into apes and pigs as punishment for violating Sabbath, as in *“We said to them be apes despised”* (2:65) and *“We said be apes despised”* (7:166). Some became pigs, and some worshipped ṭāghūt, false gods. The transformation is both literal, as some exegetes say they were physically turned into apes and pigs, and moral, as they became like apes and pigs in behaviour. The inclusion of worshippers of ṭāghūt shows that following false gods is worse than being transformed, because it is choice. The verse therefore lists three categories of worst: cursed and under wrath, transformed into apes and pigs, and worshippers of false gods.

**A Verse That Lists Worst as Warning**

This verse lists worst categories as warning not to be among them. The listing of apes and pigs refers to Sabbath violators who were transformed, as *“Be apes despised”* (2:65) and *“We made them apes despised”* (7:166). The worshippers of ṭāghūt refers to those who worship false gods, exceeding limits. The verse's purpose is to show who truly deserves resentment and punishment, not believers who believe in Allah and previous revelations. The question hal unabbi'ukum, shall I inform you, is method to draw attention to important information, as in *“Shall I inform you of worse”* (5:60). The verse ends with sharrun makānan wa aḍallu, worse in rank and farther astray, indicating that rank and path are both worse. The following verses will describe those who come saying we believe but hide disbelief, and who race to sin and consume forbidden gain, showing that some among People of Book are among worst described.
verses.61:
> When they come to you ˹believers˺ they say, “We believe.” But they are committed to disbelief when they enter and when they leave. And Allah knows what they hide

**Saying We Believe While Committed to Disbelief**

Wa idhā jā'ūkum qālū āmannā wa qad dakhalū bi-l-kufr wa hum qad kharajū bih describes hypocrisy. The same description appears for hypocrites in *“They say we believe with mouths but hearts disbelieve”* (5:41) and *“They come saying we believe”* (5:61) itself. The phrase dakhalū bi-l-kufr wa kharajū bih, entered and left with disbelief, shows that disbelief is constant, not changed by entering among believers. They enter with kufr and leave with kufr, so their saying āmannā is false. The verse therefore exposes that some People of Book and hypocrites say we believe when among believers but remain committed to disbelief when entering and leaving, showing two-faced behaviour.

**Allah Knows What They Hide**

Wa Allāhu a'lamu bi-mā kānū yaktumūn — Allah knows what they hide — seals with divine knowledge of hidden. A'lam, more knowing, bi-mā kānū yaktumūn, what they hide, yaktumūn from k-t-m, to hide, conceal, indicates they hide disbelief and plots. The same phrase appears in *“Allah knows what they hide”* (5:61) itself and in *“Allah knows what you hide and what you reveal”* (16:19). The knowledge includes hidden disbelief, hidden alliance with disbelievers, hidden mockery, as previous verses described. The verse therefore warns that saying we believe does not deceive Allah, who knows hidden. The next verse will describe racing to sin, transgression, and consuming forbidden gain, showing outward actions that match hidden disbelief. This verse describes two-faced behaviour: saying we believe when among believers, but entering and leaving with disbelief. The same behaviour appears for hypocrites who swear they are with you but are not, as verse 53 said. The phrase dakhalū bi-l-kufr wa kharajū bih, entered and left with disbelief, indicates that their disbelief is not affected by being among believers; they do not benefit from exposure to faith.

Yaktumūn, hide, from katama, to hide, conceal, is used for hiding knowledge, faith, and plots. Lisān al-'Arab defines katama as to hide, conceal. The same verb appears for hiding testimony, *“Do not hide testimony”* (2:283), and for hiding what Allah revealed, as People of Book hid descriptions of Prophet. The verse's ending with Allah knows what they hide is among verses that emphasize divine knowledge of hidden, which is basis for accountability.
verses.62:
> You see many of them racing towards sin, transgression, and consumption of forbidden gain. Evil indeed are their actions

**Racing Towards Sin, Transgression, Forbidden Gain**

Wa tarā kathīran minhum yusāri'ūna fī al-ithm wa al-'udwān wa aklihim al-suḥt describes observable racing. The three — ithm, 'udwān, suḥt — cover inward sin, outward transgression, and unlawful wealth, showing comprehensive corruption. The same trio appears in *“Racing to sin, transgression, and forbidden gain”* (5:62) itself. The racing, yusāri'ūna, indicates eagerness, not reluctance, similar to racing to disbelief in verse 41 and racing for guardianship in verse 52, showing pattern of hastening to evil. The observation tarā, you see, indicates that this racing is visible, not hidden, so believers can recognize hypocrites by actions.

**Evil Indeed Are Their Actions**

La-bi'sa mā kānū ya'malūn — evil indeed are their actions — condemns. The same condemnation appears in *“Evil are their actions”* (5:62) and in *“Evil is their inaction”* (5:63) for rabbis who do not forbid. The phrase la-bi'sa is used for strong condemnation, as in *“Evil is what they did”* (5:79) for not forbidding evil. The condemnation shows that racing to sin, transgression, and forbidden gain is not minor but evil. The verse therefore judges outward actions that correspond to hidden disbelief described in previous verse: entering and leaving with disbelief leads to racing to sin.

**A Verse That Shows Outward Signs of Hidden Disease**

This verse shows outward signs of hidden disease: those with sickness in hearts racing for guardianship (5:52) now race to sin, transgression, forbidden gain. The outward racing is visible, tarā, you see, so believers can recognize hypocrisy by actions, not only by claims. The same visibility appears for those who swear oaths they are with you but deeds void, as verse 53 said. The verse's placement after verse 61's entering and leaving with disbelief shows that hidden disbelief manifests in racing to evil. The remedy is for rabbis and scholars to forbid sinful speech and unlawful consumption, as next verse will command, indicating that leadership should prevent racing to sin.

**Why Racing Is Emphasized**

Yusāri'ūna, racing, stresses eagerness and competition in evil, as if they compete to do more sin, transgression, forbidden gain. The opposite is competing in good deeds, fa-istabiqū al-khayrāt, compete in good (5:48), which is commanded for believers. The contrast shows two races: race to evil and race to good. Believers should race to good, not to sin. The verse therefore warns against racing to evil and encourages racing to good, as earlier verses commanded seek wasīlah and strive in Allah's way.

Suḥt, forbidden gain, is defined as bribery, as Ibn Mas'ūd said, and as payment for changing rulings, as al-Ḥasan said, and as usury, as some said, all forms of unlawful wealth that strips blessing. The same term appears in verses 42 and 62 for same group, showing that consuming forbidden gain is characteristic. The phrase la-bi'sa mā kānū ya'malūn, evil are actions, appears also in verse 62 itself and is among condemnations for those who race to evil.
verses.63:
> Why do their rabbis and scholars not forbid them from saying what is sinful and consuming what is unlawful? Evil indeed is their inaction

**Evil Indeed Is Their Inaction**

La-bi'sa mā kānū yaṣna'ūn — evil indeed is their inaction — condemns inaction. The pair ya'malūn and yaṣna'ūn, both meaning to do, but yaṣna'ūn can imply crafting, making, indicating that leaders' inaction is crafted, deliberate, not accidental. The same condemnation appears in *“Evil is their inaction”* (5:63) and in *“Evil indeed was what they did”* (5:79) for not forbidding evil. The verse therefore teaches that religious leadership has duty to forbid sinful speech and unlawful consumption, and failure is evil.

**Role of Rabbis and Scholars as Entrusted Keepers**

Al-rabbāniyyūn wa al-aḥbār, rabbis and scholars, were described in verse 44 as entrusted with Book and witnesses over it, with command not to fear people but fear Me and not trade revelations for small price. Their role is to preserve, judge by, and forbid violation of Book. When they do not forbid qawl al-ithm, sinful speech, and akl al-suḥt, consumption of forbidden gain, they betray trust. The same role appears for Muslims: *“Let there be among you community inviting to good, enjoining good and forbidding evil”* (3:104) commands enjoining and forbidding. The verse therefore applies to all religious leaders, Jewish, Christian, Muslim: they must forbid evil, not ignore for fear or gain. The question law lā, why not, indicates that forbidding is expected, and its absence is blameworthy. The next verse will describe Jews saying Allah is tight-fisted, another sinful speech that rabbis should forbid but did not.

**Sinful Speech and Unlawful Consumption as Two Evils**

Qawlihim al-ithm, saying sinful, refers to sinful speech such as lying, distorting scripture, saying Allah is tight-fisted (5:64), and claiming Allah is Messiah (5:17, 72) or third of three (5:73). Aklihim al-suḥt, consuming forbidden gain, refers to bribery, usury, taking payment for distorting, as earlier defined. The two cover speech and wealth, showing that corruption is in both words and earnings. Leaders should forbid both, because sinful speech misleads people and unlawful consumption corrupts economy. The verse's pairing of qawl al-ithm and akl al-suḥt shows that they are linked: sinful speech often leads to unlawful gain, as distorting for bribery. The leaders' failure to forbid both allows racing to sin, transgression, forbidden gain described in previous verse to continue. The verse therefore links individual racing to evil and leadership failure to forbid, showing that both are needed for corruption to spread.

**A Verse That Condemns Leadership Failure**

This verse condemns leadership failure to forbid evil, which is among major duties. The same condemnation appears for Children of Israel who did not forbid one another from doing evil, as verse 79 will say *“They did not forbid one another from doing evil, evil was what they did”* (5:79). A verified ḥadīth in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (49) says whoever sees evil should change with hand, if not, with tongue, if not, with heart, and that is weakest faith, indicating that forbidding evil is duty. The verse's question law lā yanhāhum, why do they not forbid, is rebuke that should motivate leaders to forbid. The next verse will give example of sinful speech that should have been forbidden: saying Allah is tight-fisted.

The Qur'an says *“Those who were condemned among Children of Israel were condemned for disobedience and transgression, they did not forbid one another”* (5:78-79) showing that not forbidding leads to condemnation.
verses.64:
> ˹Some among˺ the Jews said, “Allah is tight-fisted.” May their fists be tied and they be condemned for what they said. Rather, He is open-handed, giving freely as He pleases. That which has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ from your Lord will only cause many of them to increase in wickedness and disbelief. We have stirred among them hostility and hatred until the Day of Judgment. Whenever they kindle the fire of war, Allah puts it out. And they strive to spread corruption in the land. And Allah does not like corruptors

**Claim That Allah Is Tight-Fisted as Insult**

Wa qālat al-yahūd yad Allāh maghlūlah reports insult: Jews said Allah's hand is tied. Yad Allāh, hand of Allah, maghlūlah, tied, chained, from gh-l-l, to tie, indicates tight-fisted, stingy, withholding provision. The claim was made when Allah withheld provision or when they were in hardship, saying Allah is stingy, as early reports say some Jews in Madinah said Allah is tight-fisted because He asks for loan, as in *“Who will lend to Allah good loan”* (2:245) and they mocked. The same claim appears in *“Jews said Allah's hand is tied”* (5:64) itself. The claim is insult to divine generosity, because Allah is openhanded, as next clause says. The Qur'an elsewhere says *“They said Allah is poor and we are rich”* (3:181) similar insult. The verse therefore records sinful speech that rabbis and scholars should have forbidden but did not, as previous verse condemned.

**Rather, He Is Openhanded Giving Freely**

Bal yadāhu mabsūṭatān yunfiqu kayfa yashā' — rather, His hands are open, giving freely as He pleases — corrects. Bal, rather, negates previous claim, yadāhu, His two hands, mabsūṭatān, open, extended, from b-s-ṭ, to extend, open, indicates generosity, openhandedness, yunfiqu, He spends, gives, kayfa yashā', as He pleases, shows that provision is by divine will and generosity, not stinginess. The mention of two hands, yadāhu, indicates vast generosity, as Arabs say openhanded with both hands. The same correction appears in *“His hands are open, He spends as He pleases”* (5:64) itself. The phrase yunfiqu kayfa yashā' shows that withholding or giving is by wisdom, not stinginess. The Qur'an says *“If Allah extended provision for servants, they would transgress in land, but He sends down in measure”* (42:27), showing that withholding is wisdom, not tight-fistedness. The verse therefore affirms divine generosity.

**Revelation Increases Wickedness and Disbelief for Many**

Wa la-yazīdanna kathīran minhum mā unzila ilayka min rabbika ṭughyānan wa kufran — what was revealed to you will increase many in wickedness and disbelief — describes reaction. The increase is not because revelation is bad, but because their reaction to it is envy and rejection, which increases existing disease, as *“In hearts is disease, Allah increased disease”* (2:10). The same phenomenon appears for hypocrites: guidance increases them in disbelief when they reject.
