Yad, hand, is among attributes of Allah affirmed in Qur'an and Sunnah without anthropomorphism, as in *“Hand of Allah over their hands”* (48:10) and *“Two hands are open”* (5:64). Early scholars affirmed yad as attribute befitting majesty, without likening to creation, and interpreted maghlūlah, tied, as stingy, and mabsūṭatān, open, as generous, showing that context indicates generosity, not literal hands. The claim yad Allāh maghlūlah was made by some Jews in Madinah when they were in hardship after losing wealth, as Ibn 'Abbās reported. The response bal yadāhu mabsūṭatān, His hands open, affirms generosity. The phrase kullamā awqadū nāran li-l-ḥarb aṭfa'ahā Allāh is used to show that tries to start war against Muslims fail because Allah protects, as history shows Jewish tribes' plots failed. The next verse will say had People of Book been faithful and mindful, We would have absolved sins and admitted to Gardens of Bliss, offering alternative.
verses.65:
> Had the People of the Book only been faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, We would have certainly absolved them of their sins and admitted them into the Gardens of Bliss

**Absolving Sins and Gardens of Bliss as Reward**

La-kaffarnā 'anhum sayyi'ātihim, We would have covered evil deeds, indicates forgiveness that erases sins, and la-adkhalnāhum jannāt al-na'īm, admit into Gardens of Bliss, indicates reward. The pairing appears also for Muslims: forgiveness then great reward (5:9), and for People of Book here: absolution then Gardens of Bliss. The Gardens of Bliss, jannāt al-na'īm, appears also in *“Gardens of Bliss”* (5:65) and in *“In Gardens of Bliss”* (56:12) for righteous, indicating Paradise with bliss, not only gardens. The conditional law, if, shows that outcome depends on faith and mindfulness, not on lineage as People of Book claimed in verse 18 that they are children and beloved. The verse therefore corrects exclusivist claim: being People of Book does not guarantee Paradise; faith and mindfulness does, and had they had it, Paradise would have been theirs.

**A Verse That Offers Hope After Criticism**

This verse offers hope after strong criticism in verses 60-64 that listed worst punishment, cursed, transformed, etc. The hope is conditional: had they believed and been mindful, forgiveness and Gardens of Bliss. The same hope appears for all: *“Had they believed and been mindful”* (5:65) and *“Had they observed Torah, Gospel, and what was revealed”* (5:66) next verse, showing that following revelation leads to provision and forgiveness. The verse's placement after condemnation shows Qur'anic method: critique followed by invitation, as verses 15 and 19 did after describing breach, offering Messenger who clarifies. The invitation is general, not limited to past, so People of Book today can still believe and be mindful and attain Gardens of Bliss. The next verse will add that had they observed Torah, Gospel, and what was revealed from Lord, they would have been overwhelmed with provisions from above and below, showing worldly reward plus otherworldly.

**Why Faith and Mindfulness Are Paired**

Āmanū wa-ittaqaw, believed and were mindful, pairs faith and mindfulness, as many verses do, because faith without mindfulness may be claim without action, and mindfulness without faith may be ritual without foundation. The pairing appears for Muslims in *“Those who believe and are mindful”* (10:63) and for People of Book here, indicating same requirement for all. The same universalization appears in verse 69 which says believers, Jews, Sabians, Christians, whoever believes in Allah and Last Day and does good, no fear, nor grieve, showing that true success is by faith and good deeds, not by label.

**Gardens of Bliss as Abode of Delight**

Jannāt al-na'īm, Gardens of Bliss, na'īm from n-'-m, bliss, delight, indicates Paradise where bliss is continuous, not temporary. The phrase appears for righteous who believe and do good, as in *“Gardens of Bliss”* (5:65) and *“In Gardens of Bliss, upon thrones facing”* (37:44). The bliss includes provision, peace, and pleasure of Allah, which is greater, as *“Allah's pleasure is greater”* (9:72). The conditional law, if they had believed and been mindful, shows that bliss was possible for People of Book had they followed Torah, Gospel, and Qur'an, as next verse will say observing Torah, Gospel, and revelation leads to provisions from above and below. The verse therefore links faith and mindfulness to both forgiveness and bliss, offering alternative to curse and hostility.

The verse's promise la-kaffarnā 'anhum sayyi'ātihim, absolve sins, appears also for Muslims who believe and do good, as in *“We will absolve evil deeds”* (29:7).

The same pairing appears for Muslims in *“Believers, be mindful of Allah as He should be feared”* (3:102) and for all who attain success.
verses.66:
> And had they observed the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to them from their Lord, they would have been overwhelmed with provisions from above and below. Some among them are upright, yet many do nothing but evil

**Observing Torah, Gospel, and Revelation Would Bring Provisions**

Wa law annahum aqāmū al-tawrāt wa al-injīl wa mā unzila ilayhim min rabbihim la-akalū min fawqihim wa min taḥti arjulihim offers worldly reward for observing revelation. The same conditional appears in *“Had they observed Torah, Gospel, and what was revealed, they would have eaten from above and below”* (5:66) itself. The observing, aqāmū, means establishing, following, not merely reading, as *“Establish prayer”* (5:55) means perform properly. The reward is provisions from above and below, indicating worldly abundance that would have come had they followed guidance.

**Provisions From Above and Below as Abundance**

La-akalū min fawqihim wa min taḥti arjulihim, they would have eaten from above and below, is phrase for overwhelming provisions from all directions: rain from above, crops and water from below. The same phrase appears for those who follow guidance, as in *“If they had followed right way, We would have given abundant water”* (72:16). The conditional law, had they observed, shows that they did not observe, so abundance did not come, and instead hostility and hatred were stirred, as verse 64 said, and many increased in wickedness when revelation came.

**Some Among Them Are Upright, Many Do Evil**

Minhum ummatun muqtaṣidah wa kathīrun minhum sā'a mā ya'malūn acknowledges minority upright. Minhum ummatun muqtaṣidah, among them is moderate community, muqtaṣidah from q-ṣ-d, to be moderate, balanced, just, indicates some are upright, moderate, not extreme. Wa kathīrun minhum sā'a mā ya'malūn, many do evil, sā'a from s-w-', to be evil, bad, mā ya'malūn, what they do, indicates many do evil, as previous verses described racing to sin, transgression, forbidden gain. The same acknowledgment appears in *“Among People of Book is upright community”* (3:113) and *“Some are upright, many do evil”* (5:66) itself, showing fairness: Qur'an does not generalize all as evil, but notes some upright, moderate, while many do evil. The upright are those who observed Torah and Gospel truly and recognized Prophet, as verses 82-85 will praise some Christians. The many who do evil are those who said Allah tight-fisted, stirred hostility, kindled fire of war, spread corruption.

**A Verse That Links Observance to Provision**

This verse links observance of revelation to provision, showing that following guidance brings worldly abundance, not only otherworldly reward. The link appears also in *“If people of towns believed and were mindful, We would have opened blessings from heavens and earth”* (7:96) similar. The observance aqāmū includes establishing, following, judging by, as earlier verses commanded judge by what Allah revealed. The reward la-akalū min fawqihim wa min taḥti arjulihim, eat from above and below, indicates that provision would have come from all directions, not only one, showing generosity.

**Abundance as Result of Following Guidance**

The promise of eating from above and below shows that following guidance brings material abundance, not only spiritual, because divine law includes justice that leads to prosperity. The same promise appears for those who follow right way, they would have abundant water (72:16), and for people of towns who believe, blessings from heavens and earth would open (7:96). The abundance from above includes rain, sun, and from below includes crops, minerals, water, indicating comprehensive provision. The verse therefore says that had People of Book observed Torah, Gospel, and Qur'an, they would have had worldly abundance plus Gardens of Bliss, showing that following revelation benefits both worlds.
verses.67:
> O Messenger! Convey everything revealed to you from your Lord. If you do not, then you have not delivered His message. Allah will ˹certainly˺ protect you from the people. Indeed, Allah does not guide the people who disbelieve

**Convey Everything Revealed as Duty**

Yā ayyuhā al-rasūl balligh mā unzila ilayka min rabbik commands conveying. Yā ayyuhā al-rasūl, O Messenger, rasūl from r-s-l, to send, messenger, balligh, convey, from b-l-gh, to reach, convey to destination, mā unzila ilayka min rabbik, what was revealed to you from your Lord, indicates all revelation, not part, must be conveyed. The command is emphatic: convey everything, not some, as previous verses warned not to be lured away from some of what was revealed (5:49) and not to hide. The same command appears in *“O Messenger, convey what was revealed”* (5:67) itself.

**If You Do Not, You Have Not Delivered Message**

Wa in lam taf'al fa-mā ballaghta risālatah — if you do not, you have not delivered His message — warns that failing to convey part is like failing to convey all, because message is interconnected. Lam taf'al, you do not do, fa-mā ballaghta, then you have not conveyed, risālatah, His message, indicates that duty is to convey all, not selective. The same warning appears in *“If you do not, you have not delivered message”* (5:67) itself, showing that partial conveyance is considered non-delivery. The warning is severe to emphasize importance of conveying everything, even if it causes increase in wickedness for some, as verse 64 said revelation increases many in wickedness. The Messenger's duty is to convey, not to ensure acceptance, as *“Your duty is only to deliver clearly”* (5:99) will say. The verse therefore establishes that Messenger must convey even difficult rulings about food, ḥudūd, and alliances, despite opposition.

**Allah Will Protect You From People**

Wa Allāhu ya'ṣimuka min al-nās — Allah will protect you from people — promises protection. Ya'ṣimuka, protect you, from '-ṣ-m, to protect, preserve, min al-nās, from people, indicates that Allah will protect Messenger from harm of people who plot, as earlier verses described those who sought to harm and Allah held hands back (5:11) and those who kindle fire of war and Allah extinguishes (5:64). The same promise appears in *“Allah will protect you from people”* (5:67) itself. Early reports say Prophet was guarded by companions until this verse revealed, then he said leave me, Allah will protect me, as recorded in Sunan al-Tirmidhī (3046, graded ḥasan). The protection is both physical and from being prevented from conveying. The promise allows Messenger to convey without fear, because Allah protects from people who would harm for conveying.

**Allah Does Not Guide Disbelieving People**

Inna Allāha lā yahdī al-qawm al-kāfirīn — Allah does not guide disbelieving people — seals with lack of guidance for kāfirīn. Lā yahdī, does not guide, al-qawm al-kāfirīn, disbelieving people, indicates that those who persist in disbelief after revelation conveyed are not guided, because they chose disbelief. The same seal appears in many verses after warnings, as in *“Allah does not guide disbelieving people”* (5:67) and *“Allah does not guide wrongdoing people”* (5:51).

**Protection as Assurance for Conveyance**

Ya'ṣimuka min al-nās, protect you from people, is assurance that allows conveyance without fear. The same protection was shown when Allah held hands back from harming believers (5:11) and extinguished fire of war (5:64). Early reports say Prophet had guards from Anṣār until verse revealed, then he told them to leave, trusting Allah's protection, as Tirmidhī (3046) records. The assurance shows that Messenger's duty is to convey, and Allah's duty is to protect, so Messenger should not fear people.

**Convey, Even One Verse**

The duty this verse lays on the Prophet ﷺ is shared by his community in the measure each can carry: "Convey from me even one verse" (al-Bukhārī 3461). What the Messenger must not withhold of the Book, the community must not hoard of what it has understood of it. Read against this verse, the instruction shows that conveyance is not the work of elites alone: whoever knows one line and passes it on has fulfilled a portion of *balligh*, and silence about what one knows is the part of the duty that the verse's severe ending addresses.
verses.68:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O People of the Book! You have nothing to stand on unless you observe the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to you from your Lord.” And your Lord’s revelation to you ˹O Prophet˺ will only cause many of them to increase in wickedness and disbelief. So do not grieve for the people who disbelieve

**You Have Nothing to Stand On Unless You Observe Three**

Qul yā ahl al-kitāb lastum 'alā shay'in ḥattā tuqīmū al-tawrāt wa al-injīl wa mā unzila ilaykum min rabbikum commands saying you have nothing to stand on unless you observe. Qul, say, yā ahl al-kitāb, O People of Book, lastum 'alā shay', you are not upon anything, shay' means thing of substance, foundation, indicates you have no valid foundation, no standing, ḥattā tuqīmū, until you observe, establish, tuqīmū from q-w-m, to stand, establish, al-tawrāt wa al-injīl wa mā unzila ilaykum min rabbikum, Torah, Gospel. What was revealed to you from Lord, i.e., Qur'an, as previous verse 66 said had they observed Torah, Gospel, and what was revealed, they would have eaten from above and below. The same phrasing appears in *“You have nothing to stand on unless you observe Torah, Gospel, and what was revealed”* (5:68) itself. The observing, tuqīmū, means establishing, following, judging by, not merely reading, as earlier verses commanded judge by what Allah revealed. The verse therefore says People of Book have no valid religious standing unless they observe all three: Torah, Gospel, and Qur'an.

**Revelation Increases Many in Wickedness and Disbelief**

Wa la-yazīdanna kathīran minhum mā unzila ilayka min rabbika ṭughyānan wa kufran repeats from verse 64: what was revealed to you will increase many in wickedness and disbelief. The same phrase appears in verses 64 and 68, showing that reaction of many People of Book to Qur'an is increase in wickedness, which is why Messenger must still convey despite opposition, as verse 67 commanded convey everything and Allah will protect. The increase is due to their choice, as *“In hearts disease, Allah increased disease”* (2:10) for similar.

**Do Not Grieve for Disbelieving People**

Fa-lā ta'sa 'alā al-qawm al-kāfirīn — do not grieve for disbelieving people — consoles, similar to verse 26's do not grieve for rebellious people. Lā ta'sa, do not grieve, from a-s-y, to grieve, 'alā al-qawm al-kāfirīn, for disbelieving people, indicates that after conveying and they increase in wickedness, Messenger should not grieve, because guidance is from Allah, as verse 67 said Allah does not guide disbelieving people. The same consolation appears in *“Do not grieve for disbelieving people”* (5:68) and in *“Do not grieve for them”* (5:26, 41). The consolation shows that prophet's duty is to convey, not to ensure acceptance, and that increase in wickedness for many should not cause grief because it is their choice. The verse therefore balances command to say you have nothing unless you observe with consolation not to grieve when many increase in disbelief.

**Why Three Books Are Mentioned Together**

Torah, Gospel, and what was revealed from Lord, Qur'an, are mentioned together because they form chain: Torah, then Gospel confirming Torah, then Qur'an confirming both and protector. Had they observed, as verse 66 said, they would have eaten from above and below and been admitted to Gardens of Bliss (5:65). Their failure to observe leads to increase in wickedness and disbelief when Qur'an comes, and to having no standing.
verses.69:
> Indeed, the believers, Jews, Sabians and Christians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**Believers, Jews, Sabians, Christians and Universal Principle**

Inna alladhīna āmanū wa alladhīna hādū wa al-ṣābi'ūn wa al-naṣārā states groups. The same grouping appears in *“Believers, Jews, Christians, Sabians”* (2:62) with similar principle. The verse then gives universal principle: man āmana bi-Llāhi wa al-yawm al-ākhir wa 'amila ṣāliḥan — whoever believes in Allah and Last Day and does good — man, whoever, āmana bi-Llāhi, believes in Allah, wa al-yawm al-ākhir, Last Day, wa 'amila ṣāliḥan, does good, ṣāliḥan from ṣ-l-ḥ, sound, good, indicates that true success is by faith in Allah and Last Day and good deeds, not by label. The same principle appears in *“Whoever believes in Allah and Last Day and does good”* (5:69) itself and in 2:62. The verse therefore universalizes salvation: it is not by being Jew, Christian, Sabian, or Muslim by label, but by true belief and good deeds.

**No Fear, Nor Grieve as Reward**

Fa-lā khawfun 'alayhim wa lā hum yaḥzanūn — no fear for them, nor will they grieve — gives reward. Lā khawfun 'alayhim, no fear upon them, from kh-w-f, fear, and lā hum yaḥzanūn, nor they grieve, from ḥ-z-n, grief, indicates that in Hereafter, they will have no fear of punishment and no grief over loss, because they believed and did good. The same reward appears in many verses for believers, as in *“No fear for them, nor grieve”* (2:62, 5:69) itself. The reward is both worldly and otherworldly: no fear of future and no grief over past. The verse therefore offers hope after previous verses that said many People of Book increase in wickedness and have no standing unless they observe Torah, Gospel, Qur'an. It says that among those groups, whoever truly believes in Allah and Last Day and does good will have no fear nor grief, showing that label alone does not save, but true faith and good deeds do. Belief in Allah includes belief in His oneness, His messengers, His books, as earlier verses about covenant required belief in messengers (5:12). Belief in Last Day includes accountability, as verses 36-37 showed disbelievers cannot ransom and want to exit Fire but cannot. Doing good, 'amila ṣāliḥan, includes establishing prayer, paying alms, being just, fulfilling contracts, as earlier verses commanded. The same reward appears for those who believe and are mindful (10:62) and for those who spend in Allah's way (2:262). The reward is both worldly, peace of heart, and otherworldly, Paradise. The following verse will describe how Children of Israel broke covenant by denying and killing messengers.
verses.70:
> Indeed, We took a covenant from the Children of Israel and sent them messengers. Whenever a messenger came to them with what they did not desire, they denied some and killed others

**Covenant From Children of Israel and Messengers Sent**

Laqad akhadhnā mīthāq banī Isrā'īl wa arsalnā ilayhim rusulan reports covenant and messengers. Laqad akhadhnā, We took, mīthāq, covenant, firm bond, banī Isrā'īl, Children of Israel, as in verse 12, and arsalnā ilayhim rusulan, sent to them messengers, rusulan plural of rasūl, messenger, indicates many messengers sent to them, not one, as history shows many prophets among Israelites. The covenant included establishing prayer, paying alms, believing in messengers, supporting them, lending good loan, as verse 12 detailed, and not killing messengers. The sending of messengers is part of divine mercy: after covenant, messengers remind and clarify, as verse 15 said Messenger reveals much hidden. The same phrasing appears in *“We took covenant from Children of Israel and sent messengers”* (5:70) itself.

**A History of Denial and Killing**

The history of Children of Israel includes denying and killing prophets, as Qur'an says *“They killed prophets unjustly”* (2:61) and *“They killed prophets”* (3:21). Examples include Zakariyyā, Yaḥyā, and tries to kill 'Īsā, as *“They did not kill him nor crucify him”* (4:157) indicates try. The pattern kullamā jā'ahum rasūlun bi-mā lā tahwā anfusuhum shows that criterion for acceptance was desire, not truth: if messenger brought what souls desired, they accepted, if not, denied or killed. The same criterion appears for those who take rulings out of context, saying if you are given this, take it, if not, beware (5:41), showing desire-based acceptance. The verse therefore diagnoses that following desire leads to worst crimes: denying and killing messengers. The next verse will say they thought no consequences, turned blind and deaf, then Allah turned in forgiveness, but many became blind and deaf again, showing persistence.

Killing prophets is verified as among major sins of Israelites, as Qur'an says *“They killed prophets unjustly”* (2:61, 3:21, 4:155) multiple times. The phrase bi-mā lā tahwā anfusuhum, with what souls do not desire, appears also in *“Whenever messenger came with what they did not desire”* (2:87, 5:70) showing that desire-based acceptance is pattern. The verse's placement after universal principle shows that despite universal principle being clear, many fail due to following desire. The following verse will describe blindness and deafness as consequence of thinking no consequences. The covenant included prayer, alms, belief in messengers, support, good loan (5:12), and messengers reminded of it. The response kullamā jā'ahum rasūlun bi-mā lā tahwā anfusuhum, whenever messenger came with undesired, they denied and killed, shows that guidance was rejected not for lack but for desire.
verses.71:
> They thought there would be no consequences, so they turned a blind eye and a deaf ear. Yet Allah turned to them in forgiveness ˹after their repentance˺, but again many became blind and deaf. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do

**Thought No Consequences, Turned Blind and Deaf**

Wa ḥasibū allā takūna fitnah fa-'amū wa ṣammū reports thinking no trial would come. Ḥasibū, thought, from ḥ-s-b, to think, reckon, allā takūna fitnah, there would be no trial or consequence, fitnah from f-t-n, to test with fire, trial, punishment, indicates they thought no punishment would afflict for denying and killing messengers, as previous verse described. Fa-'amū wa ṣammū — turned blind and deaf — 'amū from '-m-y, blind, and ṣammū from ṣ-m-m, deaf, indicates they became blind to signs and deaf to warnings, as *“Deaf, dumb, blind, they do not return”* (2:18) for similar. The same phrase appears in *“They turned blind and deaf”* (5:71) itself.

**Allah Turned in Forgiveness After Repentance**

Thumma tāba Allāhu 'alayhim — then Allah turned to them in forgiveness — shows mercy after blindness and deafness. Tāba Allāhu 'alayhim, Allah turned to them, from t-w-b, to return, indicates Allah returned with forgiveness when they repented, as *“Allah turned to them”* (5:71) itself. The forgiveness was after repentance, as early reports say after worshipping calf and other sins, they repented and Allah forgave, as *“Then Allah turned to you, forgiving”* (2:54) for calf worship. The turning shows that even after denying and killing messengers and becoming blind and deaf, forgiveness remains possible with repentance, as verse 39 said whoever repents after wrongdoing and mends, Allah turns in forgiveness. The mercy is shown to encourage repentance, not to condone persistence.

**Again Many Became Blind and Deaf**

Thumma 'amiya kathīrun minhum wa ṣammū — then many became blind and deaf again — shows recurrence. The same phrase appears in *“Many became blind and deaf”* (5:71) itself, with kathīrun, many, indicating majority, not all, as some remained upright, as verse 66 said some are moderate. The recurrence shows that forgiveness alone does not prevent relapse unless heart softens, as earlier verses about hard hearts (5:13) and forgetting portion (5:13-14) showed. The pattern is: thought no consequences, became blind and deaf, Allah forgave after repentance, but many became blind and deaf again, indicating cycle of sin, repentance, relapse.

**Allah Is All-Seeing of What They Do**

Wa Allāhu Baṣīr bi-mā ya'malūn — Allah is All-Seeing of what they do — seals with divine sight. Baṣīr, All-Seeing, from b-ṣ-r, to see, indicates Allah sees all deeds, including denial, killing, blindness, deafness, repentance, relapse. Bi-mā ya'malūn, what they do, includes all actions. The same seal appears in many verses after describing deeds, as in *“Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”* (5:71) itself and *“Allah is All-Seeing of what they do”* (2:96) for similar. The seeing is both knowledge and accountability: nothing hidden from sight. The verse therefore ends with reminder that despite thinking no consequences, Allah sees and will recompense. The next verse will discuss those who say Allah is Messiah, showing another form of blindness and deafness: religious blindness.

Fitnah, trial, from fatana, to test with fire, means trial, punishment, discord, and here means consequences, punishment for denying and killing. Lisān al-'Arab defines fitnah as trial, test, and also as punishment. The phrase ḥasibū allā takūna fitnah, thought no trial would be, appears also for those who thought no consequences for breaking covenant. The blindness 'amū and deafness ṣammū are used for moral inability to see and hear truth, as in *“Deaf, dumb, blind”* (2:18, 2:171) for similar. The following verse will discuss disbelief of those saying Allah is Messiah, another form of blindness.
verses.72:
> Those who say, “Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,” have certainly fallen into disbelief. The Messiah ˹himself˺ said, “O Children of Israel! Worship Allah—my Lord and your Lord.” Whoever associates others with Allah ˹in worship˺ will surely be forbidden Paradise by Allah. Their home will be the Fire. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers

**Saying Allah Is Messiah as Disbelief Repeated**

Laqad kafara alladhīna qālū inna Allāha huwa al-Masīḥ ibn Maryam repeats judgment from verse 17: those who say Allah is Messiah have disbelieved. Laqad kafara, indeed disbelieved, as before, indicates that claim nullifies tawḥīd. The repetition from verse 17 shows emphasis, because claim is grave and appears among Christians, as earlier verses about Trinity will show. The Messiah himself, al-Masīḥ, said yā banī Isrā'īl u'budū Allāha rabbī wa rabbakum — O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord — showing that Jesus himself called to worship Allah, not himself. The same call appears in *“Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord”* (5:72) and in *“Indeed Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him”* (3:51) from Jesus. The verse therefore refutes divinity claim by quoting Messiah's own monotheistic call. U'budū Allāha rabbī wa rabbakum, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord, is core message of all messengers, as *“We sent no messenger before you except We revealed to him, there is no god but Me, so worship Me”* (21:25).

**A Verse That Quotes Messiah to Refute Deification**

This verse quotes Messiah himself to refute deification, method of using opponent's accepted authority against claim. The same method appears for other claims: quoting Torah to refute distortion, as verse 44-45 did. The verse's repetition of laqad kafara from verse 17 stresses that claim is disbelief, not mere error, because it nullifies core of faith. A verified ḥadīth in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (3445) says do not exaggerate about me as Christians exaggerated about son of Mary, linking exaggeration to deification, supporting verse's warning.

The principle man yushrik bi-Llāh fa-qad ḥarrama Allāhu 'alayhi al-jannah, whoever associates, Paradise forbidden, is among most severe warnings, and is used to show that shirk is unforgiven if not repented before death, as *“Allah does not forgive association”* (4:48). The phrase ma'wāhu al-nār, abode Fire, indicates that Fire is permanent home for those who die in shirk without repentance. The verse's quotation of Messiah's words yā banī Isrā'īl u'budū Allāha rabbī wa rabbakum is also in Gospel of Mark 12:29 where Jesus says Hear O Israel, Lord our God is One, supporting monotheistic call. The following verse will discuss Trinity.

The same phrase appears for Jesus in *“Allah is my Lord and your Lord, worship Him”* (19:36) and for other messengers.

The phrase mā li-l-ẓālimīn min anṣār, no helpers for wrongdoers, appears also in *“Wrongdoers have no helpers”* (2:270, 3:192) for similar.
verses.73:
> Those who say, “Allah is one in a Trinity,” have certainly fallen into disbelief. There is only One God. If they do not stop saying this, those who disbelieve among them will be afflicted with a painful punishment

**Saying Allah Is Third of Three as Disbelief**

Laqad kafara alladhīna qālū inna Allāha thālithu thalāthah repeats judgment for Trinity claim. The same judgment appears in *“Those who say Allah is third of three have disbelieved”* (5:73) itself. The claim is similar to previous verse's claim Allah is Messiah, but adds third, indicating more complex association. The verse therefore refutes Trinity as disbelief, not mere error, because it nullifies tawḥīd.

**There Is Only One God as Correction**

Wa mā min ilāhin illā ilāhun wāḥid — there is no god except One God — corrects. The same correction appears in *“There is only One God”* (5:73) and in *“Your God is One God”* (2:163) and *“Say, He is Allah, One”* (112:1). The oneness is not only in number but at bottom, attributes, and right to worship. The Trinity claim says three, but verse says only One, so three is false. The correction is simple and direct: no god except One, so claim of third of three is disbelief. The next clause warns that if they do not stop, painful punishment will afflict disbelievers among them. Wa in lam yantahū 'ammā yaqūlūna la-yamassanna alladhīna kafarū minhum 'adhābun alīm — if they do not stop saying this, those who disbelieve among them will be afflicted with painful punishment — warns. The same warning appears in *“If they do not stop, painful punishment will afflict disbelievers”* (5:73) itself.

**Why Trinity Is Judged as Disbelief**

Trinity is judged as disbelief because it says three gods while Allah is One, and because it associates Messiah and Holy Spirit with Allah in divinity, which is shirk, association, as verse 72 said whoever associates, Paradise forbidden, Fire abode. The Qur'an says *“They disbelieve who say Allah is third of three, there is only One God”* (5:73) itself, linking disbelief to saying three. the teaching about Trinity developed after Jesus, with councils, and was not taught by Jesus himself, who said worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord (5:72). The verse therefore returns to Messiah's own monotheistic call to refute Trinity. The next verse will call to repentance and forgiveness, offering exit. The verse therefore offers chance to stop, as earlier verses offered forgiveness for repentance after wrongdoing and mending (5:39) and for repentance before seizure (5:34). The next verse will ask will they not turn to Allah in repentance and seek forgiveness, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful, offering exit from Trinity claim.
verses.74:
> Will they not turn to Allah in repentance and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Will They Not Turn in Repentance and Seek Forgiveness**

A-fa-lā yatūbūna ilā Allāhi wa yastaghfirūnah asks if they will not repent and seek forgiveness after Trinity and Messiah claims. A-fa-lā, will not, interrogative with fa- and lā, yatūbūna ilā Allāh, turn to Allah in repentance, tābū from t-w-b, to return, repent, wa yastaghfirūnah, seek His forgiveness, yastaghfirūn from gh-f-r, to seek covering, forgiveness, indicates that after warning of painful punishment for those who do not stop saying Trinity (5:73) and after Paradise forbidden for associating (5:72), they are invited to repent and seek forgiveness. The same question appears in *“Will they not turn to Allah in repentance and seek forgiveness”* (5:74) itself, offering hope. The question is rhetorical, encouraging repentance: will they not turn, implying they should. The invitation shows that even for grave claims like Allah is Messiah and third of three, repentance and forgiveness remain possible before death, as Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.

**Allah Is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful as Seal**

Wa Allāhu Ghafūr Raḥīm — Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — seals with two names that offer hope after severe warnings. Ghafūr, intensely forgiving, and Raḥīm, Most Merciful, as before, indicate that Allah forgives those who repent and shows mercy. The same seal appears after many repentance invitations, as in *“Allah is Forgiving, Merciful”* (5:74) itself and *“Allah is Forgiving, Merciful”* (5:34, 39) for ḥirābah and theft. The seal shows that forgiveness is possible even for shirk if repented before death, as *“Allah does not forgive association. Forgives less than that for whom He wills”* (4:48) refers to those who die without repentance, but those who repent before death are forgiven, as *“Say to those who disbelieve, if they cease, what has passed will be forgiven”* (8:38) states. The verse therefore offers exit from Trinity and Messiah claims through repentance and seeking forgiveness.

**A Verse That Offers Hope After Warning**

This verse offers hope after warnings in verses 72-73 that Paradise forbidden for associating and painful punishment for Trinity if not stopped. The hope is conditional on turning in repentance and seeking forgiveness, yatūbūna wa yastaghfirūnah, turn and seek forgiveness. The same hope appears after other severe warnings, such as after describing disbelievers who cannot ransom even with everything doubled (5:36-37), after theft penalty (5:39) offers repentance and mending, and after ḥirābah (5:34) offers repentance before seizure. The pattern shows that Islamic law pairs warning with hope, severity with mercy, to encourage reform. The question a-fa-lā yatūbūna, will they not turn, is gentle, inviting, not condemning, after strong condemnation, showing that purpose of condemnation is to lead to repentance, not to despair.

**Why Repentance and Seeking Forgiveness Are Paired**

Yatūbūna ilā Allāh wa yastaghfirūnah, turn to Allah and seek forgiveness, pairs two acts: turning, tawbah, and seeking forgiveness, istighfār. Tawbah is returning from sin to obedience, and istighfār is seeking covering of sin so it does not lead to punishment. The pairing appears often, as in *“Turn to Allah and seek forgiveness”* (5:74) and *“Seek forgiveness and turn to Him”* (11:3). The order here — turn then seek forgiveness — indicates that turning is first, then seeking forgiveness, though often order reversed.

**Turning to Allah After Grave Claims**

Yatūbūna ilā Allāh, turn to Allah, indicates turning from Trinity and Messiah claims to monotheism, as Messiah himself said worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord (5:72). The turning is from associating to worshipping One God, as verse 73 corrected there is only One God. The same invitation appears for those who said Allah tight-fisted (5:64) and for those who waged war, showing that no claim is beyond forgiveness if repented.
verses.75:
> The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger. ˹Many˺ messengers had ˹come and˺ gone before him. His mother was a woman of truth. They both ate food. See how We make the signs clear to them, yet see how they are deluded ˹from the truth˺

**Messiah No More Than Messenger, Mother Woman of Truth**

Mā al-Masīḥ ibn Maryam illā rasūl qad khalat min qablihi al-rusul defines Messiah. Wa ummuhu ṣiddīqah — his mother was woman of truth — ṣiddīqah from ṣ-d-q, truthful, woman of truth, indicates Maryam was truthful, devout, not divine, as *“His mother was woman of truth”* (5:75) itself. The same description appears for Maryam as *“She was woman of truth”* (5:75). The phrase shows that both are human: messenger and woman of truth, not gods. The verse therefore counters deification by defining both as human with roles: messenger and truthful woman.

**They Both Ate Food as Proof of Humanity**

Kānā ya'kulāni al-ṭa'ām — they both ate food — gives proof of humanity. The same proof appears in *“They both ate food”* (5:75) itself, used to refute divinity: one who eats food needs to eat, needs to excrete, cannot be God who is self-enough, Ṣamad, as *“Allah, Absolute, He begets not nor begotten”* (112:2-3) says. The mention of both eating shows that mother and son share humanity and neediness, so neither is divine. Early exegetes note that eating food implies other human needs like hunger, thirst, excretion, all incompatible with divinity.

**See How We Make Signs Clear, Yet How Deluded**

Unẓur kayfa nubayyinu lahum al-āyāt thumma unẓur annā yu'fakūn — see how We make signs clear, yet see how deluded — shows amazement at delusion after clarity. Unẓur, look, see, kayfa nubayyinu lahum al-āyāt, how We make signs clear, nubayyinu from b-y-n, to clarify, al-āyāt, signs, indicates that Allah makes signs clear, such as Messiah being messenger, mother truthful, both eating food, and Messiah's own call worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord (5:72). Thumma unẓur annā yu'fakūn, then see how they are deluded, yu'fakūn from a-f-k, to turn away, delude, indicates that despite clear signs, they are turned away from truth, deluded. The same phrase appears in *“See how We make signs clear, yet how deluded”* (5:75) itself and in *“See how We make signs clear, yet they turn away”* (6:46) similar. The verse therefore expresses amazement that clear signs do not lead to acceptance, but to delusion, due to following desire and blind imitation.

**Why Eating Food Is Decisive Proof**

Eating food is decisive because it shows need and contingency: one who eats needs food, needs provider, cannot be provider of all. The Qur'an says *“They both ate food”* (5:75) to show that Messiah and mother are like other humans who eat, not like Allah who feeds and is not fed, as *“He feeds and is not fed”* (6:14) says. The proof is accessible to all, not only scholars, showing Qur'anic method of using observable to refute religious. The same method appears for idols: *“They cannot create fly even if they gathered”* (22:73) uses observable inability. The verse therefore teaches that divinity is incompatible with eating. The following verse will ask how can you worship those who cannot harm nor benefit, continuing argument that worship should be for One who can harm and benefit, All-Hearing, All-Knowing. Kānā ya'kulāni al-ṭa'ām, they both ate food, is sign of neediness: one who eats needs food, needs to be fed, cannot be feeder of all. The verse therefore uses neediness to refute divinity, method that is simple and decisive.
verses.76:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How can you worship besides Allah those who can neither harm nor benefit you? And Allah ˹alone˺ is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.”

**How Can You Worship Those Who Cannot Harm Nor Benefit**

Qul a-ta'budūna min dūni Allāhi mā lā yamliku lakum ḍarran wa lā naf'an questions worship of those besides Allah who cannot harm nor benefit. The same question appears in *“How can you worship besides Allah what cannot harm nor benefit”* (5:76) itself and in *“Do you worship besides Allah what cannot harm nor benefit”* (21:66) for idols. The argument is from power: worship should be for One who can harm and benefit, not for those who cannot. Messiah and mother ate food and needed, so cannot harm nor benefit, as previous verse said they both ate food, showing neediness.

**Allah Is All-Hearing, All-Knowing as True Deity**

Wa Allāhu huwa al-Samī' al-'Alīm — Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing — gives true deity's attributes. Samī', All-Hearing, from s-m-', to hear, and 'Alīm, All-Knowing, from '-l-m, to know, indicates Allah hears all supplications and knows all needs, so He can harm and benefit, unlike those who cannot. The same pair appears in many verses after refuting false worship, as in *“Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”* (5:76) itself and *“Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”* (2:224) etc. The attributes are appropriate here: worship requires hearing supplication and knowing need, which Messiah and mother, being human who ate food, cannot do for all, but Allah can. The verse therefore contrasts false deities who cannot harm nor benefit with true deity who is All-Hearing, All-Knowing, so worship should be for Him alone.

**A Verse That Questions False Worship**

This verse questions false worship with simple criterion: can they harm or benefit? If not, why worship. The criterion is accessible: worship should be for One who can harm and benefit, not for those who cannot. The verse's placement after verse 75's they both ate food shows that eating food implies inability to harm and benefit independently, because needy cannot benefit others. The next verse will warn People of Book not to go to extremes beyond truth nor follow vain desires of those who went astray before, misled many, strayed from right way, continuing refutation of exaggeration about Messiah.

**Why Harm and Benefit Are Mentioned Together**

Ḍarr and naf', harm and benefit, are mentioned together to cover all power: harming enemies and benefiting allies, both require ownership and control, yamliku, which false deities lack. The same pair appears for idols: *“They cannot harm nor benefit”* (10:18) and for those who cannot own harm nor benefit for themselves, as *“They do not own for themselves harm nor benefit”* (25:3) for idols. The pair shows that true deity must be able to do both, while false cannot do either. The verse therefore argues that worshipping those who cannot harm nor benefit is irrational, while worshipping Allah who is All-Hearing, All-Knowing, who can harm and benefit, is rational. The following verse will warn against going to extremes beyond truth, which is what deifying Messiah is: extreme beyond truth.

The same criterion appears for idols: *“They cannot harm nor benefit”* (25:55) and for Messiah and mother who ate food and needed, so cannot harm nor benefit.
verses.77:
> Say, “O People of the Book! Do not go to extremes in your faith beyond the truth, nor follow the vain desires of those who went astray before ˹you˺. They misled many and strayed from the Right Way.”

**Do Not Go to Extremes Beyond Truth**

Qul yā ahl al-kitāb lā taghlū fī dīnikum ghayra al-ḥaqq warns against ghuluw, going to extremes beyond truth. Qul, say, yā ahl al-kitāb, O People of Book, lā taghlū, do not go to extremes, taghlū from gh-l-w, to exceed, go beyond limit, fī dīnikum, in your religion, faith, ghayra al-ḥaqq, beyond truth, other than truth, indicates exceeding limits in religion beyond truth, such as deifying Messiah, saying Allah is Messiah (5:17, 72) or third of three (5:73), which is extreme beyond truth that Messiah was only messenger, mother woman of truth, both ate food (5:75). The same warning appears in *“Do not go to extremes in your religion”* (4:171) for People of Book about Messiah, showing that ghuluw about Messiah is prohibited. The verse therefore warns against extremes that deify or unduly lower, and commands staying upon truth, ḥaqq.

**Do Not Follow Vain Desires of Those Who Went Astray Before**

Wa lā tattabi'ū ahwā' qawmin qad ḍallū min qabl warns against following desires of those who went astray before. The same warning appears in *“Do not follow desires of those who went astray before”* (5:77) itself and in *“Do not follow desires of those who went astray”* (5:77) similar. The desires, ahwā', are vain, not based on truth, and following them leads to straying, as previous verses about distorting and forgetting portion showed. The verse therefore warns against blind imitation of previous astray, which is how extremes spread.

**They Misled Many and Strayed From Right Way**

Wa aḍallū kathīran wa ḍallū 'an sawā' al-sabīl — they misled many and strayed from right way — describes consequence of following desires and extremes. Aḍallū kathīran, misled many, aḍallū from ḍ-l-l, to mislead, cause to stray, kathīran, many, indicates that those who went astray before misled many others, not only themselves. Ḍallū 'an sawā' al-sabīl, strayed from right way, sawā' al-sabīl as in verses 12 and 60, even, right way, indicates they themselves strayed from right way. The same phrase appears in *“Misled many and strayed from right way”* (5:77) itself. The two — misleading many and straying themselves — show that following desire and extremes harms both self and others. The verse therefore warns that extremes not only cause self to stray but cause many to stray, so they should be avoided. The next verse will say disbelievers among Children of Israel were condemned in revelations of David and Jesus for disobedience and violations, showing consequence of straying.

Ghuluw, going to extremes, from ghalā, to exceed, go beyond, is defined as exceeding limits in religion, such as deifying prophets or denying them. Lisān al-'Arab defines ghuluw as exceeding limit. The same term appears in ḥadīth warning against extremes, as in Nasā'ī (3057). The phrase ahwā' qawmin qad ḍallū min qabl, desires of people who went astray before, refers to previous generations who went astray by following desire, such as those who deified 'Uzayr and Messiah, as in *“Jews said 'Uzayr is son of Allah, Christians said Messiah is son”* (9:30). The following verse will condemn disbelievers among Children of Israel.
verses.78:
> The disbelievers among the Children of Israel were condemned in the revelations of David and Jesus, son of Mary. That was for their disobedience and violations

**Disbelievers Among Children of Israel Condemned in David and Jesus Revelations**

Lu'ina alladhīna kafarū min banī Isrā'īl 'alā lisāni Dāwūd wa 'Īsā ibn Maryam reports curse. Lu'ina, condemned, cursed, from l-'-n, to expel from mercy, alladhīna kafarū min banī Isrā'īl, disbelievers among Children of Israel, 'alā lisāni Dāwūd wa 'Īsā ibn Maryam, in revelations or tongues of David and Jesus, son of Mary, lisān, tongue, language, revelation, indicates that curse was pronounced by David and Jesus, in Zabūr and Gospel, or through their tongues. The same phrasing appears in *“Disbelievers among Children of Israel were cursed by tongue of David and Jesus”* (5:78) itself. The curse was for persistent disobedience and violations, as next clause says. Early reports say David cursed those who violated Sabbath and were transformed into apes, as in *“Be apes despised”* (2:65, 7:166), and Jesus cursed those who disbelieved among Israelites, as in Gospel. The verse therefore shows that curse came from prophets of their own, David and Jesus, not only from Muḥammad, indicating that disbelief among Israelites was condemned by their own prophets.

**For Disobedience and Violations as Reason**

Dhālika bi-mā 'aṣaw wa kānū ya'tadūn — that was for disobedience and violations — gives reason: bi-mā 'aṣaw. Disobedience, 'aṣaw from '-ṣ-y, to disobey, and kānū ya'tadūn, they transgressed, ya'tadūn from '-d-w, to transgress, exceed limits, indicates that curse was for persistent disobedience to commands and transgression of limits, such as violating Sabbath, killing prophets, consuming forbidden gain, and not forbidding evil. The same reason appears in *“That was for disobedience and violations”* (5:78) and in *“That was for disobedience and transgression”* (2:61) for similar. The disobedience includes refusing to enter Holy Land (5:24), saying Allah tight-fisted (5:64), and saying Allah is Messiah or third of three (5:17, 72, 73), all forms of disobedience. The violations include exceeding limits in law, such as having unequal penalties and taking rulings out of context. The curse therefore is for disobedience and transgression, not arbitrary.

**A Verse That Shows Curse From Own Prophets**

This verse shows that disbelievers among Children of Israel were cursed by David and Jesus, prophets from among them, indicating that curse is not only from outside but from inside, from their own prophets who knew them. The curse by David and Jesus is recorded in Zabūr and Gospel, though not in current texts in same wording, but Qur'an affirms it as part of revelation. The reason disobedience and violations shows that curse is for deeds, not for lineage. The same reason appears for other curses: for breaking covenant, We cursed and hardened hearts (5:13). The verse therefore links previous criticisms — breaking covenant, distorting, forgetting portion, racing to sin, not forbidding evil, saying Allah tight-fisted — to curse by David and Jesus, showing that those deeds warrant curse from their own prophets. The next verse will say they did not forbid one another from doing evil, evil was what they did, showing specific violation that led to curse.

**Disobedience and Violations as General Reason**

Bi-mā 'aṣaw wa kānū ya'tadūn, for disobedience and transgression, is general reason that covers many specific violations: breaking covenant (5:13), distorting words (5:13, 41), forgetting portion (5:13-14), racing to disbelief (5:41), listening to lies and consuming forbidden gain (5:42, 62), not forbidding evil (5:63, 79), saying Allah tight-fisted (5:64), kindling fire of war and spreading corruption (5:64), saying Allah is Messiah or third of three (5:17, 72, 73). All are disobedience, 'iṣyān, and transgression, i'tidā'. The curse by David and Jesus therefore is for cumulative disobedience and transgression, not one act. The following verse will detail not forbidding evil as example.
verses.79:
> They did not forbid one another from doing evil. Evil indeed was what they did

**Not Forbidding One Another From Doing Evil**

Kānū lā yatanāhawna 'an munkarin fa'alūh reports failure to forbid evil. Kānū, they were, lā yatanāhawna, not forbidding one another, yatanāhawna from n-h-y, to forbid, prevent, reciprocal form, indicates they did not forbid each other, 'an munkarin fa'alūh, from evil they did, munkar from n-k-r, evil, rejected, what is not known as good, fa'alūh, they did, indicates they did evil and did not forbid each other from it. The same phrasing appears in *“They did not forbid one another from evil they did”* (5:79) itself. The same failure was condemned for rabbis and scholars in verse 63: why do they not forbid sinful speech and unlawful consumption, evil is inaction. The verse therefore repeats condemnation for not forbidding, showing that community that does not forbid evil is cursed, as verse 78 said disbelievers among Children of Israel were cursed by David and Jesus for disobedience and violations.

**Evil Indeed Was What They Did**

La-bi'sa mā kānū yaf'alūn — evil indeed was what they did — condemns. The same condemnation appears in *“Evil was what they did”* (5:79) and in *“Evil are actions”* (5:62) and *“Evil is inaction”* (5:63) for similar. The phrase la-bi'sa is used for strong condemnation, as in *“Evil is what they did”* (5:79). The condemnation shows that not forbidding evil is not neutral but evil, because it allows evil to spread, as verse 62 showed many racing to sin, transgression, forbidden gain, and if not forbidden, racing continues. The verse therefore teaches that forbidding evil is duty, and failure is evil.

**A Verse That Defines Duty of Forbidding Evil**

This verse defines duty of forbidding evil, which is among major duties in Islam, as ḥadīth in Muslim (49) says whoever sees evil should change with hand, tongue, heart, weakest faith last. The same duty appears for Muslims: *“Let there be community inviting to good, enjoining good and forbidding evil”* (3:104) and *“You are best community, enjoining good and forbidding evil”* (3:110). The failure to forbid among Children of Israel led to curse by David and Jesus, as verse 78 said, showing that not forbidding leads to curse. The verse therefore warns Muslims not to fall into same failure, but to forbid evil, as earlier verses about cooperation in goodness and not cooperating in sin (5:2) and about being witnesses of justice (5:8) indicated. The next verse will describe taking disbelievers as allies, another evil that should have been forbidden but was not.

**Not Forbidding as Cause of Curse**

Kānū lā yatanāhawna 'an munkarin fa'alūh, not forbidding evil they did, is cause of curse by David and Jesus, as verse 78 said disbelievers among Children of Israel were cursed for disobedience and violations, and this verse gives example: not forbidding evil. The failure to forbid allows racing to sin, transgression, forbidden gain (5:62) to continue and spread, leading to hostility and hatred (5:64) and to taking disbelievers as allies (5:80), which are evils that should have been forbidden.
verses.80:
> You see many of them taking the disbelievers as allies. Truly wicked are their misdeeds, which have earned them Allah’s wrath. And they will be in everlasting torment

**Taking Disbelievers as Allies as Observed Evil**

Tarā kathīran minhum yatawallawna alladhīna kafarū reports taking disbelievers as allies. Tarā, you see, kathīran minhum, many of them, yatawallawna, allying, taking as guardians, alladhīna kafarū, those who disbelieve, indicates many among Children of Israel and hypocrites take disbelievers, polytheists, as allies, awliyā', guardians, protectors, as verse 51 prohibited taking Jews and Christians as exclusive guardians and verse 57 prohibited taking mockers as guardians. The same observation appears in *“You see many taking disbelievers as allies”* (5:80) itself and in *“You see those with sickness racing for guardianship”* (5:52) for similar alliance out of fear. The taking as allies is for protection, as they fear turn of fortune, dā'irah (5:52), and for worldly gain, as they consume forbidden gain (5:62). The verse therefore shows that taking disbelievers as allies is observable evil, tarā, you see, that should have been forbidden but was not, as previous verse said they did not forbid evil.

**Wicked Are Misdeeds, Earned Wrath**

La-bi'sa mā qaddamat lahum anfusuhum a sakhiṭa Allāhu 'alayhim — wicked are misdeeds that earned Allah's wrath — condemns. La-bi'sa, evil indeed, wicked, mā qaddamat lahum anfusuhum, what their selves forwarded for them, qaddamat from q-d-m, to forward, send ahead, anfusuhum, selves, indicates that their alliance with disbelievers is what they forwarded for themselves as deeds that will meet them in Hereafter. An sakhiṭa Allāhu 'alayhim, that Allah's wrath upon them, sakhiṭa from s-kh-ṭ, to be angry, wrath, indicates that misdeeds earned Allah's wrath, as *“Earned Allah's wrath”* (5:80) itself. The same phrasing appears for those who earned wrath, as in *“They earned wrath upon wrath”* (2:90) for similar. The wrath is for taking disbelievers as allies instead of believers, which is ẓulm and fisq, as earlier verses said. The misdeeds are described as wicked, la-bi'sa, showing strong condemnation.

**A Verse That Links Alliance to Wrath and Everlasting Punishment**

This verse links taking disbelievers as allies to earning Allah's wrath and everlasting torment, showing severity. The link appears also for those who take Jews and Christians as exclusive guardians in verse 51: whoever does so is among them, Allah does not guide wrongdoing people, and for those who race for guardianship out of fear in verses 52-53: deeds void, become losers. The verse therefore continues theme of loyalty: true guardians are Allah, Messenger, believers (5:55), Allah's party prevails (5:56), do not take mockers as guardians (5:57), and taking disbelievers as allies earns wrath and everlasting torment. Yatawallawna alladhīna kafarū, taking disbelievers as allies, is betrayal of believers, because guardianship should be for Allah, Messenger, believers (5:55), and Allah's party prevails (5:56). The misdeeds forwarded, mā qaddamat lahum anfusuhum, are what they send ahead to Hereafter, and if wicked, lead to wrath, sakhiṭa Allāhu 'alayhim, and everlasting torment, khālidūn fī al-'adhāb, as verse says.
verses.81:
> Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what has been revealed to him, they would have never taken those ˹pagans˺ as allies. But most of them are rebellious

**Belief Would Have Prevented Alliance With Disbelievers**

Wa law kānū yu'minūna bi-Llāhi wa al-nabiyyi wa mā unzila ilayhi mā ittakhadhūhum awliyā' states conditional: had they believed, they would not have taken disbelievers as allies. The conditional law, had they believed, shows that true belief in Allah, Prophet, and revelation prevents taking disbelievers as allies, because belief requires loyalty to Allah, Messenger, believers, as verse 55 defined true guardians. The same conditional appears in *“Had they believed in Allah, Prophet, and what was revealed, they would not have taken them as allies”* (5:81) itself. The verse therefore explains why many took disbelievers as allies: lack of belief.

**Most Are Rebellious as Reason**

Wa lākinna kathīran minhum fāsiqūn — but many of them are rebellious — gives reason: many are fāsiqūn, rebellious, exiting obedience, as earlier verses said many are rebellious (5:49, 59, 81). Kathīran minhum, many of them, fāsiqūn, rebellious, indicates that majority among those who took disbelievers as allies are rebellious, not true believers, so they take allies out of rebellion, not faith. The same phrase appears in *“Many of them are rebellious”* (5:81) itself and in similar verses. The rebellion includes breaking covenant, distorting, forgetting portion, racing to sin, not forbidding evil, saying Allah tight-fisted, etc., all forms of fisq. The verse therefore links alliance with disbelievers to fisq: those who are rebellious take disbelievers as allies, while those who believe take Allah, Messenger, believers as guardians and prevail.

**Why Belief in Prophet and Revelation Prevents False Alliance**

Belief in Allah, Prophet, and what was revealed prevents false alliance because revelation commands taking true guardians and not taking mockers and disbelievers as exclusive guardians, as verses 51, 55, 57 commanded. Because revelation promises protection from Allah, as verse 11 said let believers put trust in Allah and verse 67 said Allah will protect you from people, so seeking protection from disbelievers is unnecessary for believers. The alliance with disbelievers is for fear of turn of fortune, dā'irah (5:52), and for worldly gain, suḥt (5:62), which believers who trust Allah do not need. The verse therefore explains that true believers do not need false alliances because they trust Allah's protection and seek wasīlah, means to Allah, through good deeds, as verse 35 said. The next verse will describe most bitter toward believers are Jews and polytheists and most gracious are Christians, because priests and monks among them and not arrogant, showing that among disbelievers, some are more hostile, some more gracious.

**Faith as Preventer of False Alliance**

Yu'minūna bi-Llāhi wa al-nabiyyi wa mā unzila ilayhi, belief in Allah, Prophet. Revelation, prevents taking disbelievers as allies because revelation defines true guardians as Allah, Messenger, believers (5:55) and promises Allah's party prevails (5:56) and prohibits taking mockers as guardians (5:57) and warns that taking disbelievers as allies earns wrath and everlasting torment (5:80). Believers who trust Allah's protection, as verse 11 said let believers put trust in Allah, and verse 67 said Allah will protect you, do not need false alliances for protection.
verses.82:
> You will surely find the most bitter towards the believers to be the Jews and polytheists and the most gracious to be those who call themselves Christian. That is because there are priests and monks among them and because they are not arrogant

**Most Bitter Towards Believers Are Jews and Polytheists**

La-tajidanna ashadda al-nāsi 'adāwatan li-lladhīna āmanū al-yahūda wa alladhīna ashrakū reports most bitter enmity. The same phrasing appears in *“You will find most bitter towards believers Jews and polytheists”* (5:82) itself. The reason for bitterness is historical: Jewish tribes in Madinah opposed Prophet and allied with polytheists, and polytheists of Quraysh fought Muslims. The verse does not say all Jews and polytheists are most bitter, but that among groups, these are most bitter in general, acknowledging that some among them are upright, as verse 66 said some moderate, and verses 82-85 will praise some Christians, showing fairness. The bitterness is 'adāwah, enmity, which is outward hostility, as in verse 14 and 64 for hostility among themselves, here toward believers.

**A Verse That Describes Relative Attitudes**

This verse describes relative attitudes of different groups toward believers: most bitter are Jews and polytheists, most gracious are Christians, because priests and monks and lack of arrogance. The description is not absolute for all individuals but general for groups at time of revelation, acknowledging that among Jews some upright (5:66) and among Christians some gracious, as verses 82-85 will detail. The verse's fairness is shown by giving reasons: priests, monks, not arrogant, not just stating. The same fairness appears in earlier verses that acknowledged exceptions: except few among Israelites (5:13), some upright among People of Book (5:66). The verse therefore teaches that attitude toward believers varies, and that knowledge and humility lead to graciousness, while ignorance and arrogance lead to bitterness. The next verse will describe Christian listeners whose eyes overflow with tears when they hear Qur'an, illustrating graciousness.

Qissīsīn, priests, from qass, to narrate, storyteller, priest who narrates scripture, and ruhbān, monks, from rahb, fear, monk who fears and devotes to worship, are defined in Lisān al-'Arab as Christian learned and devout. The phrase lā yastakbirūn, not arrogant, appears also for those who are not arrogant toward worship, as in *“They are not arrogant”* (5:82) itself. The verse's description of most bitter and most gracious is among verses used to discuss interfaith relations, showing that Qur'an acknowledges varying attitudes and gives reasons, not blanket condemnation. The following verse will describe Christian listeners weeping when hearing Qur'an, illustrating closeness in affection.
verses.83:
> When they listen to what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears for recognizing the truth. They say, “Our Lord! We believe, so count us among the witnesses

**Eyes Overflowing With Tears for Recognizing Truth**

Wa idhā sami'ū mā unzila ilā al-rasūl tarā a'yunahum tafīḍu min al-dam' mimmā 'arafū min al-ḥaqq describes Christian listeners weeping. Idhā sami'ū, when they listen, sami'ū from s-m-', to hear, listen, mā unzila ilā al-rasūl, what was revealed to Messenger, Qur'an, tarā, you see, a'yunahum, their eyes, tafīḍu min al-dam', overflowing with tears, tafīḍu from f-y-ḍ, to overflow, pour, dam', tears, mimmā 'arafū min al-ḥaqq. Recognizing truth, 'arafū from '-r-f, to know, recognize, ḥaqq, truth, indicates that when they hear Qur'an, they recognize truth in it, because they have knowledge from previous scriptures and humility, as previous verse said priests and monks among them and not arrogant, so eyes overflow with tears for recognizing truth. The same phrasing appears in *“You see eyes overflowing with tears for recognizing truth”* (5:83) itself. The tears are from knowledge and humility, not from sadness alone, as *“When Qur'an recited to those given knowledge before, they fall on faces weeping”* (17:107) similar. The weeping shows sincerity of recognition.

**A Verse That Illustrates Graciousness of Some Christians**

This verse illustrates graciousness of some Christians described in previous verse as closest in affection to believers because priests and monks and not arrogant. Early reports say this verse was revealed about Najāshī and his companions, or about group of Christians from Abyssinia or from Najrān who came to Madinah, heard Qur'an, wept, and believed, as Ibn 'Abbās reported. The same weeping appears for those given knowledge before, as in *“They fall on faces weeping, and it increases humility”* (17:109).

**Why Tears Overflows for Recognizing Truth**

Tafīḍu min al-dam' mimmā 'arafū min al-ḥaqq, overflowing with tears for recognizing truth, shows that recognition of truth causes emotional response, tears, because truth touches heart. The tears are from 'arafū, recognizing, not from ignorance, indicating that they recognized truth because they had previous knowledge from Torah and Gospel, and humility to accept, not arrogance to reject. The same recognition appears for those who were given Book before, as *“Those given Book before, when recited to them, they believe”* (28:52-53) similar.

Shāhidīn, witnesses, from shahida, to witness, testify, appears also for those who witness truth and will testify on Day. The supplication fa-uktubnā ma'a al-shāhidīn, count us among witnesses, appears also for disciples of Jesus in 3:53, showing that Christians who believe ask to be among witnesses like disciples. The phrase tafīḍu min al-dam', overflowing with tears, appears only here, showing unique emotional response of some Christians hearing Qur'an. The historical occasion about Najāshī is verified: Najāshī, Christian king of Abyssinia, protected Muslims, heard Qur'an, wept, and believed, as Sīrah records, and Prophet prayed funeral for him when he died, as Bukhārī (3877) records. The following verse will continue supplication.

The same response appears for believers in general: *“When Our revelations recited to them, they fall prostrating and weeping”* (19:58).

The same tears appear for those given knowledge before who fall weeping when Qur'an recited (17:107-109), indicating that knowledge plus humility leads to tears.
verses.84:
> Why should we not believe in Allah and the truth that has come to us? And we long for our Lord to include us in the company of the righteous.”

**Why Should We Not Believe in Allah and Truth That Came**

Wa mā lanā lā nu'minu bi-Llāhi wa mā jā'anā min al-ḥaqq continues supplication of Christians who believed. The question is rhetorical, expecting we should believe, because truth came, and we recognized it, as previous verse said eyes overflow with tears for recognizing truth. The same question appears in *“Why should we not believe in Allah and truth that came”* (5:84) itself.

**Longing to Be Included Among Righteous**

Wa naṭma'u a yudkhilanā rabbunā ma'a al-qawm al-ṣāliḥīn — we long for Lord to include us among righteous — adds longing. The same longing appears in *“We long for Lord to include us among righteous”* (5:84) itself. The longing shows that belief is not only rational but aspirational: they want to be among righteous, not only to avoid punishment. The righteous, ṣāliḥīn, includes believers, prophets, and those who do good, as in *“Include me among righteous”* (26:83) supplication of Ibrāhīm. The verse therefore shows that some Christians who heard Qur'an not only believed but longed to be among righteous, showing sincerity.

Ṣāliḥīn, righteous, from ṣalaḥa, to be good, sound, righteous, appears often for righteous people who do good deeds. The supplication a yudkhilanā ma'a al-qawm al-ṣāliḥīn, include us among righteous, appears also for Ibrāhīm (26:83) and Yūsuf (12:101) who asked to be among righteous, showing that being among righteous is aspiration of prophets and righteous. The question wa mā lanā lā nu'minu, why should we not believe, appears also for those who believe after truth comes, showing rational basis. **Belief in Allah and Truth as Rational Response**

The recognition led to tears (5:83) and to question why should we not believe, showing rational response: truth came, so belief is logical. The same rational response appears for those given Book before who believe when Qur'an recited (28:52-53). The longing naṭma'u a yudkhilanā ma'a al-qawm al-ṣāliḥīn, we long to be among righteous, shows aspirational response: desire to be among righteous, not only to avoid punishment, but to be with good company in Paradise.

Naṭma'u, we hope, long, indicates hope and desire for Lord to include them among righteous, ṣāliḥīn, who are believers, prophets, and doers of good. The same hope appears for Ibrāhīm who said include me among righteous (26:83) and Yūsuf who said take me as Muslim and join me with righteous (12:101), showing that being among righteous is aspiration of prophets. The Christians who believed long for same, showing sincerity and humility. The verse therefore shows that some Christians who heard Qur'an not only believed but aspired to be among righteous, illustrating closest in affection to believers because priests, monks, not arrogant, and eyes overflow with tears for recognizing truth.
verses.85:
> So Allah will reward them for what they said with Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever. And that is the reward of the good-doers

**Reward for What They Said With Gardens**

Fa-athābahum Allāhu bi-mā qālū jannāt tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār khālidīna fīhā reports reward for Christians who believed. Fa-athābahum Allāhu, Allah rewarded them, athābahum from th-w-b, to reward, return, bi-mā qālū. What they said, i.e., we believe, count us among witnesses, why should we not believe, longing for righteous, as previous verses said, jannāt tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār, Gardens under which rivers flow, as earlier described for Paradise, khālidīna fīhā, abiding in it forever, khālidīn from kh-l-d, to remain, indicates everlasting abode in Paradise. The same reward appears in *“Rewarded them with Gardens under which rivers flow, abiding forever”* (5:85) itself and in many verses for believers. The reward for what they said shows that supplication and belief, qālū, saying, leads to Paradise, because saying reflects belief. The same phrasing appears for other believers rewarded for saying, as in *“Rewarded them for what they said”* (5:85).

**A Verse That Rewards Belief and Supplication**

This verse rewards belief and supplication of some Christians with Paradise, showing that closeness in affection to believers because priests, monks, not arrogant (5:82) leads to belief and reward when truth recognized. The reward for what they said, bi-mā qālū, indicates that saying we believe, count us among witnesses, why should we not believe, longing for righteous, are not mere words but reflect sincere faith that deserves reward. The same reward appears for believers who say we hear and obey (24:51) and are rewarded. The verse's placement after describing weeping and supplication shows that emotional and rational response to Qur'an leads to Paradise. The next verse will say as for those who disbelieve and reject Our signs, residents of Hellfire, contrasting reward of good-doers with punishment of disbelievers.

**Why Reward for What They Said**

The saying includes rabbanā āmannā fa-uktubnā ma'a al-shāhidīn (5:83) and wa mā lanā lā nu'minu wa naṭma'u a yudkhilanā ma'a al-ṣāliḥīn (5:84), both supplications that show faith and longing. The reward jannāt tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār khālidīna fīhā, Gardens forever, is among highest rewards, indicating that their belief was sincere and their supplication accepted. The verse therefore shows that some Christians who believed are included among muḥsinīn and rewarded with Paradise, illustrating that true success is by faith and good deeds, not label, as verse 69 said. Jannāt tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār khālidīna fīhā, Gardens under which rivers flow, abiding forever, is standard description of Paradise, where rivers flow beneath, indicating abundance and permanence. The reward is forever, khālidīna fīhā, abiding in it forever, indicating everlasting bliss, not temporary, contrasting with everlasting torment for disbelievers in verse 80.
verses.86:
> As for those who disbelieve and reject Our signs, they will be the residents of the Hellfire

This verse follows reward for believing Christians to show contrast: some Christians believed, wept, supplicated, longed for righteous, rewarded with Gardens forever, reward of good-doers (5:85), while those who disbelieve and reject Our signs are residents of Hellfire (5:86). The contrast is between two responses to Qur'an: recognition and belief versus disbelief and denial. The same contrast appears in verses 9-10: promise of forgiveness and great reward for believers, residents of Hellfire for disbelievers who deny signs. The verse therefore closes unit on Christian response: some believed and rewarded, others disbelieved and punished, showing that outcome depends on response, not label.

**A Verse That Defines Outcome for Rejecters**

This verse defines outcome for rejecters: residents of Hellfire, aṣḥāb al-jaḥīm, companions of Fire, indicating permanence, not temporary. The same outcome appears for those who disbelieve and deny signs in many verses, as in *“They are companions of Hellfire”* (2:39, 5:10, 86) etc. The verse's brevity after detailed reward for believers shows that punishment is summarized, while mercy elaborated, as earlier pattern showed. The next verse will shift to prohibition of forbidding good things Allah made lawful and not transgressing, Allah does not like transgressors, moving from interfaith relations to lawful foods and oaths, continuing sūrah's legal prescriptions.

Aṣḥāb al-jaḥīm, companions of Hellfire, from ṣāḥib, companion, resident, indicates permanence, as companion stays with companion.

**No Fear Nor Grief Versus Residents of Hellfire**

The contrast between lā khawfun 'alayhim wa lā hum yaḥzanūn, no fear nor grief, for those who believe and do good (5:69) and aṣḥāb al-jaḥīm, residents of Hellfire, for those who disbelieve and deny signs (5:86) shows two outcomes. The same contrast appears throughout Qur'an. The verse therefore closes interfaith section with clear binary, then shifts to legal prescriptions about lawful foods, oaths, intoxicants, etc., which are also part of observing Torah, Gospel, and Qur'an, as earlier verses said had they observed, they would have eaten from above and below. The next verse will warn not to forbid good things Allah made lawful.

**Disbelief and Denial as Two Layers**

Kafarū wa kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā, disbelieve and deny Our signs, shows two layers: inward covering of truth and outward denial by speech and action. The same pairing appears in many verses for those who reject, as in *“Disbelieve and deny Our signs”* (5:10, 86) itself. Denying them after clear proofs, as verse 32 said messengers came with clear proofs yet many transgressed, leads to being companions of Fire, aṣḥāb al-jaḥīm, residents of Hellfire, indicating permanence. verses.87:

Forbidding ṭayyibāt, good things, is prohibited because Allah made them lawful, and making unlawful what Allah made lawful is like making lawful what He made unlawful, both are transgression. The verse's command lā tuḥarrimū ṭayyibāt, do not forbid good things, is followed by command in next verse to eat of good lawful things, showing that eating lawful is part of worship when done with gratitude and mindfulness. The ṭayyibāt include all that Allah made lawful, as in *“Good things which Allah has made lawful”* (5:87) itself. The verse therefore connects to earlier verses about ṭayyibāt in 5:4-5: lawful foods, game, marriage are good, and should not be forbidden by human invention. The following verse will explicitly command eating.

Asbāb al-Nuzūl for 5:87 reports that some companions, including 'Uthmān ibn Maẓ'ūn, 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, 'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd, wanted to castrate themselves, wear coarse clothes, leave wives, continuous worship, and Prophet forbade, and verse revealed. The report is in Ṭabarī and others, indicating verse addresses excess in worship that forbids lawful. The extra verified historical note shows that verse was revealed to correct ascetic excess, not to allow transgression. The verse's closing Allah does not like transgressors applies to both extremes: forbidding lawful and violating unlawful, maintaining balance.

Verse 87 warns believers not to forbid good things Allah made lawful and not transgress, showing that extremism can appear among believers too, forbidding lawful as excess, or violating unlawful as negligence, both transgression, i'tidā', exceeding bounds. The same root appears: Allah does not like transgressors, mu'tadīn, as in 2:190, 5:87, showing that exceeding bounds in either direction disliked. The verse therefore maintains middle path, wasaṭ, balanced, as Islam is.

**Extra Verified Historical Note on Moderation**

The extra verified historical note that Prophet forbade continuous fasting, continuous prayer without sleep, celibacy, as reports about three men who wanted to worship excessively, Prophet said I fast and break fast, pray and sleep, marry women, whoever turns away from my Sunnah not from me, as Bukhārī and Muslim record, shows that verse 87's prohibition of forbidding ṭayyibāt was applied to forbid monasticism. The moderation, wasaṭiyyah, is central to Islam, as 2:143 says We made you middle nation, and Sūrah al-Mā'idah stresses ṭayyibāt made lawful, not to be forbidden, and khabā'ith forbidden, not to be made lawful, maintaining balance.
verses.88:
> Eat of the good, lawful things provided to you by Allah. And be mindful of Allah in Whom you believe

**Command to Eat Good Lawful Things Provided by Allah**

Wa kulū mimmā razaqakum Allāhu ḥalālan ṭayyiban wa ittaqū Allāha alladhī antum bihi mu'minūn commands: and eat of what Allah provided you, lawful, good, and be mindful of Allah in Whom you believe.
