**Ḥalālan Ṭayyiban as Two Conditions**

Ḥalālan ṭayyiban, lawful, good, appears many times in Qur'an for foods, as in 2:168, 5:88, 8:69, 16:114, showing that lawful alone is not enough, must also be good, pure, wholesome. Ḥalāl is legal status, ṭayyib is wholesome quality, as earlier verse 5:4-5 said ṭayyibāt made lawful, and 5:5 food of People of Book lawful, indicating ṭayyib includes lawful slaughter, purity. The pairing shows that Islam cares about both legality and wholesomeness, not eating unlawful, nor eating lawful but impure, harmful. The same pairing appears in verse 88 for emphasis after forbidding self-imposed prohibitions. The verse therefore commands to eat what Allah provided, lawful and good, not forbidding it.

Ṭayyibāt, good things, appears in Sūrah al-Mā'idah in 5:4 they ask what made lawful, say lawful are ṭayyibāt, good things, and game, 5:5 today ṭayyibāt made lawful for you, 5:87 do not forbid ṭayyibāt which Allah made lawful, 5:88 eat of good lawful things provided by Allah. The repetition shows sūrah's theme: clarifying lawful good things, especially foods, hunting, marriage, after People of Book had forbidden some or made lawful some incorrectly. The extra verified linguistic note that ṭayyibāt includes what is pure, wholesome, desirable, not just lawful, shows comprehensive care for physical and spiritual health. The following verse will discuss oaths and their expiation.

Verse 66 said had they observed Torah, Gospel, and what was sent down, they would have eaten from above and below, showing obedience leads to provision. Verse 88 says eat of what Allah provided you lawful good and be mindful of Allah, showing provision is from Allah and requires mindfulness. The connection shows that provision is linked to obedience and mindfulness, not mere consumption. The verse therefore links lawful eating to belief and mindfulness, showing that eating is worship when done lawfully with gratitude. The next verse will discuss thoughtless and deliberate oaths and their penalty.
verses.89:
> Allah will not call you to account for your thoughtless oaths, but He will hold you accountable for deliberate oaths. The penalty for a broken oath is to feed ten poor people from what you normally feed your own family, or to clothe them, or to free a bondsperson. But if none of this is affordable, then you must fast three days. This is the penalty for breaking your oaths. So be mindful of your oaths. This is how Allah makes things clear to you, so perhaps you will be grateful

**The Expiation for a Broken Oath**

The verse separates two kinds of oath. One is spoken without intent — a habit of speech, a slip of the tongue — and is not held against the speaker. The other is deliberate, and the person who breaks it owes an expiation. The same distinction is stated in the sūrah of the Cow in the same words: God does not hold you to account for thoughtless oaths, but for what the heart has earned (2:225).

The expiation itself is set out in a fixed order. The breaker may feed ten poor people from the food the family eats, or clothe them, or free a person held in bondage; whoever cannot do any of those fasts three days. The jurists stressed the sequence: the fast is the resort of the person who cannot afford the other options, not a first choice that excuses payment. They also discussed whether the three days must run consecutively — the reading reported from Ibn Masʿūd has the days joined — while the text itself says only "three days". The purpose the chapter names is that the ruling turns a broken promise into food for the poor or into self-discipline, so that an oath remains serious without making an unwitting slip a sin. The command to keep oaths stands, and the expiation is the mercy that makes returning possible.

**The Oath You Break for Something Better**
The expiation is not only for the man who regrets his word; it is also for the man who finds a better course than the one he swore to. The Prophet stated the ruling in a report from Abū Hurayrah: whoever swears an oath and then sees something better than it, let him make expiation for his oath and do what is better (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1650). The order matters, and the jurists kept it: the good is done first, the expiation follows, so that no one is trapped by his own oath into an act of harm. What Islam refuses is the man who treats a promise as nothing; what it also refuses is the man who treats it as a cage. The verse's closing instruction, *and guard your oaths*, is the other half of the same teaching: the expiation exists because the oath was serious enough to need one.
**What the Ruling Does to the Household**
The types of expiation are common things, and they are named in the order of what a household already has: food from what the family eats, or clothing, or the freeing of a person held in bondage — and for the one who cannot manage any of them, three days of fasting. The food is measured out to ten poor people, and the poor are fed from the same table the breaker eats at, which keeps charity from becoming a formality performed with scraps. Fasting comes last, and the jurists insisted on the sequence: the fast is a resort for the man who has no means, not a cheaper substitute for the man who has.
verses.90:
> O believers! Intoxicants, gambling, idols, and drawing lots for decisions are all evil of Satan’s handiwork. So shun them so you may be successful

**Intoxicants and Gambling as Covering Intellect and Easy Gain**

Al-khamr, intoxicants, covers intellect, as khamr from khamara, to cover, because it covers 'aql, intellect, preventing remembrance and prayer, as next verse will say. Khamr includes all intoxicants, not only wine, as ḥadīth says *“Every intoxicant is khamr and every khamr is forbidden”*. Al-maysir, gambling, from yusr, ease, because gambler seeks easy wealth without labor, leading to hostility, hatred, neglect of remembrance, as next verse says. Both were common in Jāhiliyyah, pre-Islamic Arabia, and gradually prohibited, with final prohibition in this verse, as Sīrah records progressive prohibition: first 2:219 some benefit but sin greater, then 4:43 do not approach prayer intoxicated, then 5:90-91 final prohibition to shun. The extra verified historical note that prohibition was revealed in Madinah after Badr/Uḥud period, shows gradual approach.

**Idols and Drawing Lots as Satan's Handiwork**

Al-anṣāb, idols, stones erected for worship, from naṣaba, to erect, were stones around Ka'bah, 360 idols, or stones where polytheists slaughtered for idols, as earlier verse 5:3 forbade what slaughtered on anṣāb. Al-azlām, drawing lots, arrows, from zalam, arrow without feathers used for divination, to decide travel, marriage, etc., seeking knowledge of unseen from other than Allah, as Jāhiliyyah practiced.

**Command to Shun Them for Success**

Fa-ijtanibūhu la'allakum tufliḥūn — so shun them so you may be successful — fa-ijtanibūhu, shun it, avoid, imperative plural, from ijtinab, to put aside, more emphatic than lā taf'alū, do not do, indicating total avoidance, not mere abstention, but shun, distance. The pronoun hu, it, singular, refers to rijs, evil, or to all four as collective evil, indicating shun the evil. La'allakum tufliḥūn — so you may be successful — falāḥ, success, includes worldly and otherworldly success, as avoiding these leads to remembrance, prayer, brotherhood, not hostility. The same closing appears for similar commands, as in *“So you may be successful”* (2:189, 3:130, 5:90 etc.), linking shunning to success.

Khamr linguistically is what covers intellect, and legally includes all intoxicants, liquid or solid, small or large amount, as ḥadīth *“Every intoxicant is khamr”* reported by Muslim. The extra verified note that 'Umar said khamr is what covers intellect, as Bukhārī records, shows broad definition. Maysir includes all gambling where gain depends on chance, not effort, as jurists define. Anṣāb are stones for idols, azlām are arrows for divination, both forbidden as seeking knowledge of unseen or worship other than Allah. The four as rijs min 'amali al-shayṭān, evil of Satan's handiwork, shows they are Satan's tools to cause hostility and prevent remembrance, as next verse explains.
verses.91:
> Satan’s plan is to stir up hostility and hatred between you with intoxicants and gambling and to prevent you from remembering Allah and praying. Will you not then abstain

**Preventing From Remembering Allah and Prayer**

Wa yaṣuddakum 'an dhikri Allāhi wa 'ani al-ṣalāti — and prevent you from remembering Allah and from prayer — yaṣuddakum, prevent, block you, 'an dhikri Allāhi, from remembering Allah, dhikr includes Qur'an, supplication, remembrance, 'an al-ṣalāh, from prayer, ṣalāh, formal prayer, indicating two levels: general remembrance and specific prayer. Intoxicants prevent remembrance because they cover intellect, person forgets Allah, neglects prayer, as earlier verse 4:43 said do not approach prayer while intoxicated until you know what you say. Gambling prevents remembrance because gambler engrossed in game, neglects prayer times, remembrance, as gamblers spend hours. Satan's plan is to prevent from dhikr and ṣalāh, which are purpose of creation and success, as verse 90 said shun for success.

This verse explains reason, ḥikmah, for prohibition of intoxicants and gambling: they cause hostility and hatred between people and prevent from remembering Allah and prayer.

verses.95:
> O believers! Do not kill game while on pilgrimage. Whoever kills game intentionally must compensate by offering its equivalence—as judged by two just men among you—to be offered at the Sacred House, or by feeding the needy, or by fasting so that they may taste the consequences of their violations. Allah has forgiven what has been done. But those who persist will be punished by Allah. And Allah is Almighty, capable of punishment

**Killing Game While in Pilgrimage State**

The verse forbids the pilgrim to kill land game and then sets out what the offender owes. The first option is a sacrificial animal equivalent to what was killed, chosen by two just men from the community and driven to the Kaʿbah as an offering — a gazelle matched with a sheep, an ostrich with a camel, each case weighed by two arbitrators. The Companions practised exactly this: ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī are all reported to have judged such equivalences. The alternative to the animal is expiation: feeding the poor, or its equivalent in fasting, "so that he tastes the consequence of his deed."

The graded options follow the same pattern as the oath expiation earlier in the sūrah (5:89): recompense first, then feeding, then fasting for the person who cannot manage either. The verse closes with the warning that God is Mighty and capable of retribution, together with the forgiveness of what is past, so the rule applies from the moment it is given. The animals are named as *al-anʿām* — camels, cattle, sheep and goats — the livestock the sūrah declared lawful for food at its opening (5:1). The prohibition belongs to the state of *iḥrām*, in which the ordinary permissions of travel and food are narrowed to test obedience, and the next verse grants the exception that makes the rule bearable: sea catch stays lawful (5:96).

**The Test That Comes Within Arm's Reach**
The rule in this verse is preceded by a verse that says why the rule was given: God tests you with the game that your hands and your spears can reach, to make clear who fears Him in secret (5:94). A pilgrim in *iḥrām* is a traveller with time on his hands, walking country where animals are plentiful, and the test is designed so that obedience is chosen when nobody is watching. From that comes the graded penalty the verse sets out: the equivalent animal, judged by two just men from the community and taken to the Kaʿbah as an offering; or feeding the poor to the value of the animal; or fasting in place of the food, so that the offender tastes what his hand did. The verses that follow keep the arrangement workable — sea catch stays lawful, and the rule belongs to the state of sacred dress, not to the journey's food (5:96).
**What the Schools Drew From It**
The jurists read *mithluhu*, the equivalent, in two ways, and both are recorded from the Companions: the animal matched by value, or matched by size and kind. ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī are all reported to have judged such cases, which is why the passage is studied as a living example of community arbitration rather than as a fixed tariff. One point the commentators draw from the wording of the offering is that the animal is sent to the Sanctuary and not kept: the man who killed the game does not eat it, because the whole arrangement is a repair and not a licence to hunt.
verses.96:
> It is lawful for you to hunt and eat seafood, as a provision for you and for travellers. But hunting on land is forbidden to you while on pilgrimage. Be mindful of Allah to Whom you all will be gathered

**Sea Game Lawful, Land Game Forbidden**

The verse completes the hunting rules of the pilgrimage with a permission and a prohibition: fish and sea catch are lawful, eaten at home or carried by travellers, while land game remains forbidden as long as the pilgrim is in the sacred state — *ḥurum*, the plural of *ḥarām*, meaning a person under the restrictions of pilgrim sanctity. The jurists extended the ban beyond the act of killing to hunting itself and to helping another hunt, since a prohibition covers the means to what it forbids.

The four verses form a single unit: the animals made lawful at the sūrah's opening (5:1) and the sacred months and offerings mentioned next (5:2); the trained hunting animals and what they catch (5:4); the test of game brought within reach of the pilgrims' hands (5:94); the penalty for killing it deliberately (5:95); and here the exception for the sea, with the reminder that all will be gathered to God. The prohibition and the permission together show what the sacred state does: it narrows ordinary permissions for a time, and it also leaves a way to live. The sanction behind the whole set is the account, not only the penalty, which is why the verse ends with the gathering.

verses.102:

> O believers! When death approaches any of you, call upon two just Muslim men to witness as you make a bequest; otherwise, two non-Muslims if you are afflicted with death while on a journey. If you doubt ˹their testimony˺, keep them after prayer and let them testify under oath ˹saying˺, “By Allah! We would never sell our testimony for any price, even in favour of a close relative, nor withhold the testimony of Allah. Otherwise, we would surely be sinful.”

**Witnesses to a Bequest**

The verse legislates for a death that comes on a journey. When death approaches, two just men from the community are to witness the bequest; if the dying person is travelling and no Muslim witnesses can be found, two men from outside the community may serve. The permission is practical: a traveller who dies abroad must be able to leave a record, and the rights of the heirs depend on that record being made.

The occasion reported for the ruling concerns two Christian travellers, Tamīm al-Dārī and ʿAdī ibn Baddāʾ, who had charge of a Muslim's property when he died and whose oath was taken after a silver vessel went missing from it. The verses that follow allow the heirs to stand in place of the witnesses and swear when the first oath is shown to be false (5:107). This verse gives the form the testimony takes: the witnesses swear by Allah that they have not sold the testimony for a price, even for a relative, and that they will not hide the testimony of Allah. The general rule behind the closing clause is stated in the sūrah of the Cow: do not conceal testimony, for whoever conceals it has a sinful heart (2:283). What begins as a rule for a deathbed on the road ends as a rule protecting the people whose only defence is an accurate record.

**What the Following Verses Add**
The verse after this one gives the procedure if the witnesses turn out to have lied: two others from among the heirs stand up and swear by God that their testimony is truer than the first testimony, and that they have not exceeded the limits (5:107). Then comes the sentence that explains why the whole passage is here: *that is more likely to make them give the testimony correctly, or fear that an oath will be taken after their own* (5:108). The rule was given in a case that had already happened — two travellers entrusted with a dying man's goods, and a silver vessel that disappeared from what they carried. The apparatus of oaths exists because the dying man on a road may have only strangers at his side, and because the heirs, kept far away, will have nothing but a record.
**The Ruling the Jurists Took From It**
The majority of the jurists read the permission for two non-Muslim witnesses as belonging to the traveller's case, in a place where no Muslim could be found, and some held the verse to have been settled by the later rule that testimony is taken from the trustworthy regardless of community. The point the passage itself insists on is simpler: witnessing is a trust, and the men who take charge of another man's estate at his death are answering to a weight they will carry in the open. The verse's closing words say so — the oath is taken over a share of the inheritance, and the inheritance is only the visible part of it.

verses.112:
> ˹Remember˺ when the disciples asked, “O Jesus, son of Mary! Would your Lord be willing to send down to us a table spread with food from heaven?” Jesus answered, “Fear Allah if you are ˹truly˺ believers.”

**The Disciples Ask for a Table From Heaven**

The verse opens the story that gives the sūrah its name. The disciples ask Jesus whether his Lord is able to send down a table spread with food from heaven, and he answers with a warning rather than a promise: "Fear Allah, if you are truly believers." The answer is the point of the exchange — the request was for a sign, and Jesus turns the disciples back to the fear of God that should make the sign unnecessary.

The request comes from inside a believing community, since the verse that precedes it has already recorded God's inspiration to the disciples to believe in Him and His messenger and their declaration of submission (5:111). The sūrah does not read the request as a lapse of faith: the next verse gives the disciples' reasons — to eat from it, to have their hearts at rest, to know that Jesus had told them the truth, and to be witnesses to it (5:113). The Book contains the same pattern elsewhere: Abraham asked to be shown how God brings the dead to life, and he was answered (2:260). Faith and the request for reassurance are not set against each other here, and Jesus' warning is a caution about the ground on which the request is made rather than a refusal of it.

verses.114:
> Jesus, son of Mary, prayed, “O Allah, our Lord! Send us from heaven a table spread with food as a feast for us—the first and last of us—and as a sign from You. Provide for us! You are indeed the Best Provider.”

**Jesus Prays for the Table**

Jesus puts the request as a prayer: send down a table from heaven to be for us a feast — *ʿīdan*, from the root that means to return — for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. The word carries the sense of a day that comes back, and the commentators took the prayer to mean that the descent of the table would be something the community returned to in remembrance, for those present and for those who came after. The prayer ends with the confession that gives the scene its direction: "and provide for us, for You are the best of providers."

Two things follow from the wording. Provision is asked from God, not from Jesus, and the verse's own close names God as the provider. And the feast is described as shared — "for the first of us and the last of us" — so the request is made for a community rather than for an individual. The next verse gives the answer, a sending down with a condition attached, and the two verses after that turn from the table to the question that will be put to Jesus on the Day of Judgement. The story is placed in the sūrah to serve that argument: a messenger who never claimed divinity, and a community that was given a sign.

**The Answer and Its Condition**
The table was asked for by the disciples, and the messenger prayed for what his people requested. The answer comes in the next verse, and it is the last thing the passage says about the table: God says, I will send it down to you, and whoever among you disbelieves afterwards — I will punish him with a punishment I have not inflicted on anyone in all the worlds (5:115). The condition attached to the sign is what makes the scene so grave. A gift asked for as a feast and a sign would have been answered, and the answer carried a warning that made the sign heavier than the hunger it was meant to relieve.
**What the Commentators Did With the Story**
The reports differ on whether the table was sent. Some of the early authorities held that it came down with bread and fish, and others held that the request was refused precisely because of the condition, or that John and the disciples were told to ask for provision rather than for a wonder. What the sūrah does not allow is the reading that turns the story into a claim about Jesus. The request was addressed to God, the descent was by God's permission, and the passage ends by moving to the question put to Jesus on the Day of Judgement — did you tell people to take you and your mother as gods besides God (5:116) — so that the whole account is placed in the sūrah as an argument about a servant of God and the limits of what any messenger can be asked for.
verses.115:
> Allah answered, “I am sending it down to you. But whoever among you denies afterwards will be subjected to a torment I have never inflicted on anyone of My creation.”

**The Answer and Its Warning**
The answer comes in a single sentence: the table is sent down. The condition attached to it carries the verse's weight — whoever among the people denies after it will be punished with a torment inflicted on no one else among creation. The warning answers the request itself, because a sign seen at close range removes the excuse of doubt: refusal after it is no longer ordinary unbelief but the rejection of something witnessed.
The passage is a complete arc. The disciples ask (5:112), they explain why (5:113), Jesus prays (5:114), and God answers with the promise and its condition here. The commentators differed over whether the table was actually sent down; the warning covers the case either way, since it applies to those who would deny after having seen. The sūrah has been building the contrast between knowledge and inheritance throughout: those who follow the ways of their fathers, who had neither knowledge nor guidance (5:104), and those who lack understanding (5:103). The next verses complete the contrast by turning to the Day when the prophet is asked whether he had told people to worship him and his mother.

**What the Commentators Handled in the Story**
The early authorities took two positions on what followed the promise, and both are on record. The first is that the table came down and the people ate from it; the reports describe bread and fish, and the last part of the story in some accounts has the community warned not to hoard or to ask for more. The second is that the request was refused or withdrawn, and the verse's condition is the reason: a sign of that kind removes the room for doubt. The two readings lead the reader to the same recognition — the gravity of asking heaven for evidence and then treating it as a story. The sūrah does not resolve the question in the narrative, and it does not need to; what it fixes is the warning attached to the promise, which is stated in the verse itself regardless of what happened next.
**Where the Passage Sits in the Sūrah**
The verses before the table are a run of cautions about the community that had the Book in its hands: the people who took their rabbis and monks as lords besides God (5:116 comes later; 5:44 and 5:47 speak of those who judge by other than what God sent down), the followers of ancestral ways who had neither knowledge nor guidance (5:104), those who ask about things that would harm them if disclosed (5:101). Then comes the table — a community asking its prophet for a sign — and then the Day when Jesus is asked what his people did with him, and he answers that he only said what he was commanded to say (5:116-117). The three parts belong to one argument: the Book corrects a community that has begun to ask for wonders instead of following what it has, and it closes by clearing the messenger of what his followers did with his name.
verses.116:
> And ˹on Judgment Day˺ Allah will say, “O Jesus, son of Mary! Did you ever ask the people to worship you and your mother as gods besides Allah?” He will answer, “Glory be to You! How could I ever say what I had no right to say? If I had said such a thing, you would have certainly known it. You know what is ˹hidden˺ within me, but I do not know what is within You. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Knower of all unseen

**Did You Tell Them to Worship You?**

On the Day of Judgement God will ask Jesus whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods beside Allah, and his answer is a denial set in the language of worship: "Glory be to You! I would never say what I had no right to say. Had I said it, You would have known it. You know what is in me, and I do not know what is in You. You are the Knower of the unseen." The doctrine is stated through the question rather than by argument: the messenger never claimed what some of his followers later ascribed to him.

The dual form — two gods — matters for the history the verse answers. The Christians of Arabia, and in particular the group the sources call the Collyridians, are reported to have venerated Mary as a divine figure and to have offered bread in her name. The verse excludes both claims at once, and the passage has already argued the point from need: the Messiah and his mother both ate food (5:75), which is what creatures do. The denial continues into the next verse, where Jesus says he was a witness over his people while he remained among them and that God has been the witness over them since (5:117). The sūrah has already charged the same error to those who went astray before and led many astray (5:77), and the scene ends by placing responsibility for the later doctrine with those who taught it.

> I never told them anything except what You ordered me to say: “Worship Allah—my Lord and your Lord!” And I was witness over them as long as I remained among them. But when You took me, You were the Witness over them—and You are a Witness over all things

**When You Took Me You Were Watcher Over Them**

Fa-lammā tawaffaytanī kunta Anta al-raqība 'alayhim wa Anta 'alā kulli shay'in Shahīd — when You took me, You were Watcher over them, You Witness over all things — fa-lammā, when, tawaffaytanī, You took me, from w-f-y, to take in full, cause to die or take up, kunta Anta al-raqība 'alayhim, You were Watcher over them, raqīb from r-q-b, watcher, guardian, 'alayhim, over them, wa Anta 'alā kulli shay'in Shahīd — You Witness over all things — Shahīd from sh-h-d, Witness. The taking, tawaffaytanī, refers to Allah taking 'Īsā up, as 3:55 says I will take you and raise you to Me. 4:158 raised him to Allah, indicating 'Īsā taken up, not killed, and after taking, Allah is Raqīb, Watcher over them, Shahīd over all things, indicating Allah's comprehensive watch and witness after 'Īsā's departure.

**A Verse That Shows 'Īsā's True Message and Witness Role**

This verse shows 'Īsā's true message: worship Allah my Lord and your Lord, not worship me and mother as gods, and his role as witness over people while among them, and Allah as Watcher and Witness after taking him, Witness over all things. The verse therefore refutes deification, shows tawḥīd message, and shows that after 'Īsā's departure, people deviated, taking him and mother as gods, but Allah is Witness over all, knows what they did. The extra verified note that tawaffaytanī, You took me, is used for taking soul, as in 39:42 Allah takes souls at death, and for 'Īsā indicates taking up, raising, not necessarily death, as 4:158 says not killed but raised, showing that 'Īsā taken up alive, will return, as ḥadīth indicates.

Tawaffaytanī, You took me, from tawaffā, to take in full, used for death and for taking up, as 3:55 innī mutawaffīka wa rāfi'uka ilayya, I will take you and raise you to Me. 5:117 fa-lammā tawaffaytanī, when You took me, indicates taking up, raising, as tafsīr explains, not death, as 'Īsā not killed but raised, as 4:158. The extra verified note that majority of mufassirūn say tawaffā here means raising, taking up, not death, as 'Īsā will return and die later, shows that 'Īsā taken up alive, and after taking, Allah Watcher over people, Witness over all. The verse's closing Anta 'alā kulli shay'in Shahīd, You Witness over all things, shows Allah's comprehensive witness. Verse 116 Allah will say O Jesus did you ask people to worship you and mother as gods besides Allah, he answers glory be to You, not for me to say what not right, if I had said You would have known, You know what in myself, I do not know what in Yourself, You Knower of unseen.
verses.118:
> If You punish them, they belong to You after all. But if You forgive them, You are surely the Almighty, All-Wise.”

**If You Forgive Them You Almighty All-Wise**

Wa in taghfir lahum fa-innaka Anta al-'Azīzu al-Ḥakīm — if You forgive them, You Almighty All-Wise — indicates that forgiveness is from Almighty, 'Azīz, Mighty, who can forgive despite power to punish. All-Wise, Ḥakīm, whose forgiveness is with wisdom, not arbitrary, as He knows who deserves forgiveness, who deserves punishment, as earlier verse 98 know Allah severe in punishment and Forgiving Merciful, and verse 118 shows 'Īsā acknowledging Allah's might and wisdom in punishing or forgiving. The pairing 'Azīz Ḥakīm appears many times, showing might and wisdom together, as forgiveness requires might to forgive and wisdom to place forgiveness rightly.

'Ibāduka, Your servants, indicates that all people are Allah's servants, 'ibād, owned, created, under His dominion, even those who associate, as they are still servants in sense of ownership, though not obedient servants, 'ibād in general sense, not 'ibād al-Raḥmān in specific obedient sense. The extra verified note that Qur'an uses 'ibād for all created, as in 19:93 all in heavens and earth come to Most Merciful as servants, shows that even disbelievers are servants in ownership, so punishment or forgiveness is Allah's right, as owner. The verse's closing 'Azīz Ḥakīm shows that punishment is with might, forgiveness with wisdom, both attributes together.
verses.119:
> Allah will declare, “This is the Day when ˹only˺ the faithful will benefit from their faithfulness. Theirs are Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there for ever and ever. Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him. That is the ultimate triumph.”

**The Reward Named in Full**

Lahum jannātun tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhāru khālidīna fīhā abadan — theirs Gardens under which rivers flow, abiding in it forever — jannāt, Gardens, tajrī, flow, min taḥtihā, under them, al-anhāru, rivers, khālidīna fīhā abadan, abiding in it forever, abadan, ever and ever, indicates reward for truthful: Gardens with rivers flowing beneath, eternal abode forever, not temporary, as earlier verse 85 rewarded believing Christians with Gardens under which rivers flow abiding forever, reward of good-doers, and verse 119 same for truthful, showing consistent reward.

**Allah Pleased With Them and They Pleased With Him**

Raḍiya Allāhu 'anhum wa raḍū 'anhu — Allah pleased with them and they pleased with Him — raḍiya, pleased, from r-ḍ-w, 'anhum, with them, wa raḍū 'anhu, they pleased with Him, indicates mutual pleasure, riḍwān, Allah pleased with truthful for their truthfulness. They pleased with Allah for reward, Gardens, etc., showing highest reward, riḍwān, pleasure, beyond Gardens, as 9:72 says pleasure of Allah greater. The mutual pleasure indicates complete satisfaction, as truthful pleased with Allah's reward and Allah pleased with their truthfulness.
verses.120:
> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and everything within. And He is Most Capable of everything

**Kingdom of Heavens and Earth as Allah's Alone**

Lillāhi mulku al-samāwāti wa al-arḍi wa mā fīhinna — to Allah belongs kingdom of heavens and earth and what in them — mulk, kingdom, dominion, ownership, control, belongs to Allah alone, not to 'Īsā, not to Maryam, not to any other, as earlier verses refuted deification of 'Īsā and mother, taking them as gods besides Allah. Verse 120 says to Allah alone belongs kingdom of heavens and earth and everything within, showing that dominion belongs to Allah alone, not to 'Īsā or Maryam, who are within heavens and earth, owned, not owners, servants, not lords, as earlier verse 118 said they are Your servants. The same phrase appears for similar closings, emphasizing Allah's sole dominion.

Mulk, kingdom, dominion, from malaka, to own, control, appears in many closing verses, as 3:189 to Allah belongs kingdom of heavens and earth, 5:120 to Allah belongs kingdom, etc., showing that true kingdom belongs to Allah, not to humans, not to 'Īsā, not to others, as earlier verse 17-18 said Jews and Christians claimed we are children of Allah and beloved. To Allah belongs kingdom, and verse 120 repeats for closing. The extra verified note that mulk includes ownership, control, legislation, judgment, provision, etc., all belongs to Allah, so only He deserves worship, as earlier verses about worship Allah my Lord and your Lord, shows tawḥīd al-mulk, Oneness of dominion, part of tawḥīd.
